illustrations.ocrText: By the grammatical standards of Pirahã discourse, he had no business speaking at all. https://3quarksdaily.com/3quarksdaily/2026/01/of-grammar-and-truth-language-models-and-norms-truth-and-the-world.html?utm_source=flipboard&utm_content=topic/cognition In the 1980s, when the linguist Daniel Everett went to live with the Pirahã people of the Amazon, he had a mission: to translate the Bible into their language and convert them to Christianity. What he discovered, however, was something he hadn't anticipated. The Pirahã didn't exactly reject his religious message. They just couldn't take him seriously. The problem, as Everett eventually came to understand, was grammatical. Pirahã requires speakers to mark the source of their knowledge. When you make a claim about something, you have to indicate whether you witnessed it directly, heard it from someone else, or learned it in a dream. This isn't an optional rhetorical flourish. It's as obligatory as verb tense in English. Everett had not seen Jesus himself. He knew no one who had. And he wasn't reporting a dream. illustrations.ocrText: How to Read Impact Estimation Tables 4. Never Add Columns Blindly Purpose Impact Estimation Tables are decision tools, not predictions. 1. Read Vertically (Values First) Each row answers: "How well does this strategy help us move this value toward its goal?" If a critical value has no strong impacts, the strategy set is incomplete. 2. Read Horizontally (Strategy Personality) Each column answers: "What kind of strategy is this really?" • Few rows → focused, specialist strategy • Many rows → systemic, architectural strategy 3. Ignore Precision, Look for Direction The numbers are: • Explicit • Debatable • Replaceable by data later What matters is relative impact, not false accuracy. Strategy impacts: • Interact • Overlap • Sometimes cancel out Always check dependencies and synergies. 5. Tie Every Cell to Cost and Risk A high-impact cell is meaningless unless: • Cost is known • Risk is explicit • Learning is planned 6. Use Tables to Design Evo Steps Good strategies: • Deliver value early • Reduce uncertainty • Earn the right to invest more Bottom Line If it can't be shown in an Impact Estimation Table, it isn't ready for board-level decision-making. They just need to know they can 'drill down' into detail, as we do with accounting. Built-in to VIE is a wide range of ways of simplifying the decision basis [Simple]. In ValPlan app, there is an automatic one-page summary of the top-ten, or critical-ten values. The basic VIE Cell can have more or less detail, depending on needs, although the detail can be retrieved with a single click, as needed. illustrations.ocrText: The Principle Of 'Quality Quantification' The Words of a 'Lord' "All qualities can be expressed quantitatively, 'qualitative' does not mean unmeasurable". illustrations.ocrText: In the Cleanroom Method, developed by IBM's Harlan Mills (1980) they reported: • "Software Engineering began to emerge in FSD" (IBM Federal Systems Division, from 1996 a part of Lockheed Martin Marietta) "some ten years ago [Ed. about 1970] in a continuing evolution that is still underway. • Ten years ago general management expected the worst from software projects - cost overruns, late deliveries, unreliable and incomplete software • Today [Ed. 1980!], management has learned to expect on-time, within budget deliveries of high-quality software. illustrations.chapterTitle: QC Rules for Top Level Objectives
illustrations.caption: This slide presents four quality-control rules for writing top-level objectives in Planguage specification practice. It lists the CLEAR, UNAMBIGUOUS, and QUANTIFIED QUALITY principles on the left, and the NO DESIGN rule (rule 4) on the right with an illustrative photograph of a collapsed building showing the consequences of architectural defects when design is confused with quality requirements.
illustrations.ocrText: QC Rules for Top Level Objectives • CLEAR: Every word and phrase should be clear enough to allow objective test of a delivery. (we need to know exactly what is required and expected) • UNAMBIGUOUS: Every word and phrase should be unambiguous to all potential intended readers. (no different than intended interpretations should be possible) • QUANTIFIED QUALITY: all qualities (good things we want to improve) shall be expressed quantitatively. • After we started the exercise I regretted not adding the usual rule: • 4. NO DESIGN: objectives shall not be expressed in terms of a design or architecture – (a 'means' to reach the 'real' objective), when it is possible and is our real intent, to express the improvements in terms of quality and cost that are instead. Potential consequence of major defects in architecture specs www.Gilb.com

illustrations.ocrText: 12 Tough questions:© Tom Gilb http://www.gilb.com/DL24 1. Numbers Why isn't the improvement quantified? 2. Risk What is the degree of risk or uncertainty, and why? 3. Doubt Are you sure? If not, why not? 4. Source Where did you get that information? How can I check it out? 5. Impact How does your idea effect my goals and budgets, measurably? 6. All critical factors Did we forget anything critical to survival? 7. Evidence How do you know it works that way? Did it 'ever'? 8. Enough Have we got a complete solution? Are all requirements satisfied? 9. Profitability first Are we planning to do the 'profitable things' first? 10. Commitment Who is responsible for failure, or success? 11. Proof How can we be sure the plan is working, during the project, early? 12. No cure, no pay Is it 'no cure, no pay' in a contract? illustrations.ocrText: Principles of 'Dynamic Design to Requirements' 1. MEASURE: It is easier to measure accurately than to predict accurately. 2. ADJUST: It is faster to adjust a bad design, than to figure out the right design to begin with. 3. SMALL: Even small systems can be complex, so frequent incremental measurement of progress is smart. 4. INTERACTIONS: Everything can interact with everything else, now and in future, so incremental measurement of critical factors is the only safe way to keep score. 5. DtC: It is better to 'design to a cost' you require, than to 'estimate a design cost' you can't afford. 6. DIV: It is easier to 'design to a stakeholder value level' than to just hope your design will meet that level. 7. ESTIMATE EARLY: Estimation of design impacts, helps sort out 'probably good design' early. 8. CONFIRM: Only measurement of design value-delivery and design-costs will confirm you got it right. 9. DESIGN CONFLICT: Designs interact with all other system designs, past and future, compounded by changing stakeholder needs - and consequent re-design. 10. DESIGN STEPWISE: Small incremental steps of design, greatly simplify understanding of complex design. Copyright gilb.com 2019-2023. Robe

MAYBE MORE THAN ONE DESIGN IS A GOOD IDEA? We have, up to now, used the simplification 'a design to cost' (perhaps also the verb, 'to design to cost'). In some circumstances, one brilliant design idea (fix a low price in the contract) can do the job, as I have often experienced in my consultancy. But, the more complex and sizeable the system, the more unlikely that a 'single brilliant design' will get us to the cost levels we want. And even if a single idea did get us to an initial defined cost target, then ambition, motivation and competition, and opportunity - might suggest that additional design ideas, might be able to lower a cost, even more. illustrations.ocrText: The Penta Model The Penta Model [65, 2022-2023] that Al Shalloway and I developed, is a direct result of our dislike of the conventional and misleading 'Iron Triangle' ideas. A good-enough design, can simultaneously improve everything. The limit, as Musk reminds us [29, MM], are laws of nature. With 'Penta', we can apply a set of ideas, to clarify the top level of the 'reality of everything'. We bring in Resources to cover all manner of resources, not just 'Budget and Schedule'. We bring in Value, to include all manner of qualities, and of other stakeholder values. We bring in 'design' (with its many attributes) as the tool for managing Values and Costs. We bring in 'Efficiency' (a synonym for Productivity [66]), in order to emphasize a higher aspiration level, the general aspiration, of most projects, products, and change processes. And 'Efficiency' ties together all the other Penta elements, especially: Efficiency = ∑Values : ∑Costs. Scope Values Designs Efficiency Resources The engineering and costs relationships are complex, but manageable with a systematic and multi-dimensional approach to sorting things out, over time, incrementally. illustrations.ocrText: 'Relative %' impacts A neutral % metric - for a 'big picture' We let our spreadsheet convert from the Scale-Units to another metric: the '% increment' towards the target level. At first this might seem like just another way to say the same thing. It is, but this 'other way' has a very useful property, which the Scale-Units do not. We can fairly meaningfully add them up for different values and costs. This gives us a better overall picture, of all the impacts, that a single strategy has. And in addition, we can add up the % impacts of a set of different but complimentary strategies, and decide if we have enough design ideas; or better, we can see if we have enough impacts with a safety margin. These capabilities make it worthwhile, to introduce the % impact, and the computations required for it are automated. And 20 minutes saving, is equivalent to 50% of the way between Past and Goal (65 - 25 = 40, 20/40 = 50%). illustrations.ocrText: Bar Chart Presentation Bars are good Publicity One simple way of visualizing an estimated numeric-value impact, and the estimated cost consumption, is a Bar Chart. We need to do the ground work, to make it happen. I. e. Quantifying the Value impact goals, clarifying the Means, and estimating the degree of 'Means impact'. This is the process of developing the numbers, which can then be translated into the bar-chart visual-representation; so we can sense and see good effects, and poor effects, at a glance. At a later stage, when strategies are actually incrementally implemented, and their real impacts are measured, we can present the comparison of estimates versus reality in side-by-side bar charts. The 'Day 3' in Fig. B refers to our startup planning process [7, SW] which we use with clients. Day 1 Value quantification, Day 2 Strategy specification, Day 3 Value Impact Estimation. Day 4 selection of next week's incremental-value-delivery sub-strategy. So the IE process is a one-day quick-and-rough evaluation; designed to help us quickly find a 'pretty smart' value delivery, for next week (real system, implementation and feedback). illustrations.ocrText: Iron Triangles (IA) Why the Iron Triangle is a misleading 'cost teaching'. 1. The Iron Triangle teaching (IA) does not contain any ideas about multiple Qualities, and multiple costs. 2. IA does not contain any ideas about quantification of the quality ideas. It is likely to be a one-dimensional concept of 'quality', and may be (implied, not defined), something like 'product defects', even that - badly defined. 3. IA does not recognize the idea of a 'design', (by any synonym, like strategy, architecture), and the ignores fact that designs have multiple qualities, and costs aspects. Like food for example. And that a design process can improve all factors simultaneously. 4. IA does not recognize the idea of cost-effectiveness, or efficiency (E = ∑V : ∑C). It seems to assume something like the one-and-only-quality should be 'high enough', and you have to choose to meet a deadline (Schedule) or a Budget. And if that is not possible, your only tactic is to reduce Scope (Functionality, 'what the system does'). 5. Our counter suggestion is the, hopefully, more-realistic Penta Model [65]. illustrations.ocrText: When are this book's 'Cost Management' ideas, 'too advanced'? 1. These Cost Engineering (CE) ideas are primarily intended for large and complex systems. For example Military, Government [15, Gov], Space, Manufacturing, Health, Aircraft Safety. They (CE) are not intended for projects where costs are not a major issue, nor intended 'where cost overruns can be swallowed by big purses, and costs are a minor part of that environment's big picture'. 2. We can start by drawing some kind of 'line in the sand'. Anything which takes less than a year, less than 10 people, and less than the cost of 10 people is probably small enough, that 'old conventional methods' are satisfactory. 3. But, money and time aside, if the project when badly managed, might result in the loss of a single life, or in serious medical conditions, then it would seem 'better methods' are then worth considering. 4. This does raise an interesting question, whether our Cost Engineering ideas can be simplified, or scaled down, so that their cost is trivial, and their benefits worthwhile. illustrations.ocrText: How can this book's Cost Management ideas, be simplified'? [7, Startup Week] and [52, SP] & [81, Sim] 1. STAKEHOLDERS: [11, SE] Larger projects might need to analyze 100 or more stakeholders, each of which have 2 or more requirements. But, although a small project might actually have such a volume of stakeholders, even a single human does. Here is a useful simplification. Agree on your top-ten stakeholders, listed on a single page. Make sure you go well beyond the usual 'user and customer' stakeholders, and include suppliers, contracts, laws, and competitors. This will force you to be conscious of some 'too costly' stakeholders! 2. REQUIREMENTS: [78, VR] Then (after Stakeholders) analyze just the top-ten stakeholders, to find the most critical requirement for each one of them. The top 10 requirements. And simplify each one, to 'Tag/Scale|Goal'. That at least, makes you to quantify the critical Value requirements. This will make you to sense that some of your most ambitious Goal levels can be too costly. This includes specific 'cost reduction' requirements. 3. illustrations.ocrText: 10.0.6 Then.... Automate Step 5, Automate. "An important part of this is to remove in-process testing after the problems have been diagnosed; if a product is reaching the end of a production line, with a high acceptance rate, there is no need for in-process testing". Musk admitted he made a big mistake by too much automation in the initial Tesla Model 3 production line ("Production Hell", he called it). He succeeded, by getting rid of many of the robots,. Productivity was better, in some cases without automation! Step 5 refers to the fact that there were many automated tests in the Model 3 production line, which were necessary initially, to sense problems in the process. But which were superfluous, when things were running more smoothly, and which could be productively replaced, by only measuring final results. The main point he is making, by positioning automation as the 5th step, is that we should only automate, 'the right stuff'. illustrations.ocrText: 1.1 Stakeholders [4] Why stakeholders first? Your stakeholders are those who will help you with better resilience, and also those who will be affected by resilience problems. You need to analyze them, and their needs and capabilities; to make a good resilience system, based on a good resilience plan. It is illogical to jump in to Resilience Technology itself, as people seem to be prone to. Your Resilience Plan must satisfy your adopted set of Resilience Objectives: and it is your Stakeholders that determine those objectives. Only when your Resilience Objectives are clear and accepted, can you decide how effective the Resilience Strategies will be for them. There is no 'general resilience'. There is only, and primarily, the resilience that your organization (Stakeholders, and Objectives) needs: and it must be tailored to your organisation itself. illustrations.ocrText: 2.1 Value Objectives What 'exact stake' do the stakeholders have? What is it we have to achieve (Value Objectives!) with our Resilience strategies? It is not enough to merely identify a stakeholder value with a generic 'name Tag', such as 'Resilience'. There are infinite possible misunderstandings of what that value really is. We need to get a clear idea of the value, so nobody can misunderstand it. It may be difficult to analyze, or find out exactly, what a group of diverse stakeholders 'value'. They might not even have a clear idea of it themselves. But, it is important to try to get a clear idea, to try to verify that the idea is reasonable, and sane. And even if we are bound to be wrong to some degree: it needs to be clear and unambiguous. It is bad enough that we will have difficulty figuring our exactly what the value is. But we need not compound the problem, by allowing many other people to misinterpret, it in vastly different directions. Do not give them the opportunity to screw things up. Reserve that for yourself. illustrations.ocrText: 2.2 Value Objectives - Ambition Level The stakeholder 'Ambition' level The first rough approximation of what the stakeholder expects. There are many levels of possible specification, for a 'stakeholder value objective'. Each added specification level has its uses. Each component of the overall value specification gives us more insight. The better the value specification, the more likely we are to get a satisfactory set of Resilience Strategies, and thus to satisfy the stakeholders reasonably well. The Value 'Tag' is the first level of definition. It usually clarifies a great deal, but also leaves a great deal of possibility for misinterpretation. The next level of specification, I call the 'Ambition' level. It is a sentence of about 10 words, which details the level of value, needed by the stakeholder, well enough for simple small systems. But not well enough for larger systems. TO DO: for each Value, write, after the Tag (all Caps) a new line Ambition: And specify the best stakeholder ambition level you can find for them. illustrations.ocrText: Ambition Level: a statement needing much better definition We are used to starting with a 'Tag' and a rough statement, intended to be a 'full definition' of the Tag name. The problem is we typically stop there. To eliminate ambiguity, more structure and detail is required, such as a Scale of Measure and a Target level ('Wish'). They will be derived from this unstructured and ambiguous Ambition Level definition. Not easy, but necessary! An example of ambiguous, ambition level definition, is the INCOSE definition of 'Adaptability'. Status 5 Wish 50 Status [Failure Cause = External Hackers, System Type = Government IT System] @ 18 Fe The Scale icon is an arrow emerging from a system junction, describing how well the system functions. Like 'how Resilient' it is. If your resilient system is non-trivial; and you would probably not need this book if it were trivial; then you absolutely must define your stakeholder values, better than the 'Ambition level'. Unfortunately far too many critical and large systems, stop at that Ambition level. We believe that lack of clarity, and engineering rigor is a primary cause of system failure. [7, Bent]. Engineering begins with metrics (Scale), not poetry (Ambition level). illustrations.ocrText: 2.7A Other Competing Objectives with 'Resilience' Objectives Like Usability, Safety Unfortunately, Resilience is not the only problem we need to solve in our system. It is not the only high priority and critical objective for our system. It is in fact just a nasty newcomer, to our pile of problems we had before. Which we were very bad at mastering, before. If you were to list the top-10 critical stakeholder-objectives for your system, the Resilience might make it to the top-10 list. But that means that there are 9 other critical objectives; and 'critical' means - any one of them can blow up your business or organization totally. In rough terms, that means Resilience can only get access to 10% of the IT systems resources. Yet, it could theoretically swallow 1,000 % (10X+) of the available resources, to do everything first class. Resilience resource needs are near infinite. That means that your resilience project will never get the resources needed to 'Make Resilience Great Again'. Never. So, shall we give up, and 'hope for the best'? We can do something. We can do better. We can try to be cost-effective: i. e. getting the 'most resilience for the resources allocated'. 'Best Effort'.

illustrations.ocrText: 5.2B Workshop Analysis: Estimating side-effects What we hope you observed or learned: 1. You cannot live in a Resilience bubble. Your Resilience Planning will affect other critical values (Qualities) of the system. Like it or not. 2. You then have a choice: Think about the side effects of your designs early (pro-active engineering), or react too late (incurring costs and delays) 3. Even simplified specification and estimates are a tool for seeing potential problems, and potentially dealing with them earlier. Not everything must be 'discovered' or 'learned' after the fact. 4. There is an underlying engineering truth: designs can be changed to modify undesired side-effects. Why is this important? • This is part of your potential methods for taking that 'whole systems' viewpoint, which many people correctly emphasise, is necessary, to avoid sub-optimisation • The Resilience Engineer, needs to be a focused specialist. But the 'system architect' and 'project managers', by contrast, need to see the whole system, and deal with that totality. illustrations.ocrText: 6.2B Workshop Analysis: 'Estimate Costs or other Resources What we hope you observed or learned 1. You cannot make use of strategies, that lie outside your share of the budget 2. There is no such thing as 'we can or will pay any price for improved levels of Resilience'. 3. The costs are a 'known unknown' until actually estimated. Then their reality, could be big enough, to destroy your entire system. One nuclear bomb can ruin your entire day. 4. It is possible to make rough estimates, and then later it is possible to either 'adjust the design to be cheaper' (design to cost, re-design to cost), or to 'increase the budget or deadline', if it seems worth doing 5. Why is this important? • Decision-makers, and resource holders (CFO), should never give 'go ahead' to high-tech, for large complex systems, without some understanding of estimated costs, and a specific means for controlling those costs in practice. • Practical Example: Delivering 5% of the value in increments and measuring real costs (EVO [2], Dynamic Design to Cost, IBM Cleanroom/Mills and Quinnan [http://concepts.gilb.com/dl896]. Estimates are always difficult, but they are useful. What we are trying to teach, with this workshop exercise 1. We are trying to teach multi-dimensional thinking. How to juggle many balls simultaneously. Difficult, but, realistic, and possible - using tools like the Impact Estimation Table; which gives a better understanding of the possible 'reality to come'. 2. We are trying to teach an engineering method: logic and fact-based thinking for planning. This planning is then followed up with plenty of feedback, from incremental value deliveries, to adjust rough plans, to align them with reality. illustrations.ocrText: 8.4 Workshop Analysis: 'Identify Risks' What do we hope you noticed in this workshop exercise? 1. Initial drafts of planning specifications will contain many un-intended defects. 2. You have to review your drafts, or get someone else to do it. 3. The effort needed to clarify things is probably much smaller than the effort needed to fix the misinterpretation of the implementation of those things. Failure has dire, possibly life-threatening, consequences. • If you really are going to take any responsibility for Cyber Resilience planning, you need to increase your level of discipline so you are able to produce seriously effective results.

Withstand | Continue essential mission functions despite adverse conditions | Adverse conditions include, but are not limited to, successful execution of an attack by an adversary. Recover | Restore mission functions during and after the adverse conditions | Adverse conditions include, but are not limited to, successful execution of an attack by an adversary. Evolve | Change mission functions and/or supporting capabilities, so as to minimize adverse impacts from actual or predicted adverse conditions | Adverse conditions include, but are not limited to, successful execution of an attack by an adversary. illustrations.ocrText: G14: Evolution I am starting to notice a pattern, in the set of Means Objectives. Compare with Adaptability, Anticipate, Agility. They all seem to be about the degree of development of the system to deliver resilience. I have a growing feeling this is overdone. We could probably have one Means Objective about capability, building more capability. And then focus on asking ourselves if there are other means Objectives, related to Resilience, that we are missing, which are critical (for example Usability, Maintainability, Safety, Testedness, Availability, Security). In any case I am just working on this set of Means Objectives to give some ideas, and the real Resilience Planners need to figure ut the set of critical objectives which are importantfor them, in their environment. Not copy this set uncritically. The thing I am trying to do is to provide many examples so readers and student can get some ides of how to clearly specify Resilience Objectives. illustrations.ocrText: ACCURACY AND PRECISION CONCEPTS Target patterns of shots fired by two riflemen. The left pattern shows low precision and high accuracy with large random errors. The right pattern shows low accuracy and high precision with large bias (systematic error). DEGRADED OPERATION Again we want to stress from the outset that the real world cannot be usefully described in black and white terms. The real world of data processing consists of what could be called "grey areas": different shades of grey, ranging from black to white. If we are to design realistic systems and control their quality in a realistic manner, then we must make a habit of thinking in terms of "degrees" of quality of our systems. The designer of a large and complex computer file, let us call it a "data base", may be worried that some error in the data base may cause such a high risk of undesireable results that he is forced to consider the data base, and thus his entire system, to be in a failed state. Nothing "works" from the system user point of view until the data base data is "repaired" and the entire related system can be put "on the air" again.

illustrations.ocrText: In many practical situations, it may be impossible to ever guarantee that the data base is "perfect". The system designer is quickly forced to consider a design whereby the total system can function in a reasonable manner, even if parts of it are a bit "sick". This is not very far from the way our body operates, or the way in which many organizations operate. They may be partly "sick" but they continue to function in a less than ideal mode. It has been conventional for many years to design computer hardware to operate in what has been called "fail soft" mode. When certain classes of errors occur, the machine - or parts of it - continue providing a limited class of service to the user, rather than no service at all. The limitation may be that the reaction time of the system is increased, or it may be that certain types of service cannot be provided. The same principles of degraded operation can be consciously designed into the "soft" (logic and data) parts of computerized systems. However, just as with hardware systems, this does not happen by chance. The designer must quite consciously design a degraded mode of operation into his programs and data designs. LOGICWARE: program logic which actively processes data and 2. DATAWARE: data structures which contain information, which are themselves passive, but which are actively altered by logicware. The two terms are appropriately captured in the term "DATA PROCESSING". Each has certain properties which are independent of the other, yet, like the marriage of hardware and software, they must normally be combined to give us a useful result. MULTIDIMENSIONAL ATTRIBUTES MEASURED: METRICS Quality control in real data processing systems invariably means control over many different system characteristics. For example space, speed, maintainability, reliability, system adaptability, system implementation effort, etc. to name a few general quality characteristics.

It is imperative in the making of a relevant system design that the goals of such a design are clearly stated. Design goals are always expressed, in practical terms, as multi-dimen- sional goals. These are usually all sub-goals of the concept of a "good" system, but it is nevertheless necessary to break the larger and more general goals down into smaller and more measurable goal concepts. Many of the terms used to describe system goals can have varied meanings to different observers. It is therefore necessary, for clear communication of design goal ideas, to define these goals in such a way that they can be objectively measured in practice with controllable accuracy. The first step is often to specify a theoretical metric such as the idea of a VOLT. The next step is a practical measuring device such as the magnetically driven mechanical needle voltmeter. illustrations.ocrText: The major concept employed is that the team is responsible for the quality of the work produced just as the football team is responsible for the goals or victories produced. The individuals must find ways of working together so as to satisfy the team objective of success in their work. The "EGO" of the individual is satisfied through group success and his contribution to group success. The team itself is not dependent on the survival of any one individual. Full appreciation of the team idea comes from integration within the guidelines of readable source code ("structured programming" and top down design and implementation are some of the techniques employed to further this objective) and also by the concept of "review committees" (or "inspections"). illustrations.ocrText: Technique: Logically linked record organization Also called: primary chain, linked records, pointer chain. DESCRIPTION Each individual record contains a reference to another record in the file. The entire files records may be accessed by means of a sequence of logically linked records. A simple sequence of logically linked records. Record "A" is the first logical record. Record X is the last, indicated by a traditional zero pointer. IMPORTANT VARIATIONS a. The simplest variation of linked record organization The basic variation involves a single simple sequence. The pointers allow direct access to the next record without additional programming at the application programmer level. These are usually a logical relative record number (from 1, 2, 3, ... to n-th record) which allows the basic file software, usually part of the operating system, to access the record. b. overflow area In the basic variation, new records are either added on to the end of the sequence (by changing the zero pointer to a reference to the new record), or they are not added except as part of a major reorganization of the file, or they are added in logical (but not physical) sequence thereby lowering efficiency.

B C N INDEX TO FILE RECORDS FILE RECORDS N A basic identifier index to a file. IMPORTANT VARIATIONS: INDEXED FILE a. Direct pointer The index consists of a table, each element of which contains at least two sub-elements: an identifier and a direct pointer to the record associated with that identifier. A direct pointer is usually a relative record number which the basic file handling software can use to find the record by means of a SEEK or the basic file handling software can use to find the record by means of a SEEK or READ type operation, using that pointer as a parameter. A direct pointer may point to a particular record, but an important variation is that it points to a group (or the beginning of a group) of records. These records may themselves be indexes, and a hierarchy of indexes may be created. 170

illustrations.ocrText: Technique: Position by key DESCRIPTION Each record is placed in the relative record position which corresponds to its major key (identifier). Knowing the key allows us to retrieve the corresponding record using direct access to the relative record. If necessary an arbitrary sequence of records is assigned an artificial identifier based on the relative record position it holds. ADVANTAGES No index, pointers or complex key conversion algorithms are needed. DISADVANTAGES If the key already exists and is not consecutively used, then space will be wasted for unused keys. EXAMPLES If a collection of records is stable in nature and space and speed savings are important, then this technique is attractive. In particular, when a temporary file, such as "todays transactions" is allocated, then the transaction reference number can be conveniently made equal to a relative record number (perhaps modified by the date, for example: 740417. 000001 referring to the first record for that date in relative sequence). illustrations.ocrText: PART VI Selected data base design technology Techniques: Data base design DEFINITION: A DATA BASE is a particular sort of file. There are no extremely clear boundary lines between data bases and other types of files, but data bases are characterized by being more complex than simple files, in the following areas: a. several record structures or types in the same file (as viewed by the operating system. Each record type may seem like a separate file to the application programmer). b. the possibility of multiple users trying to access and update the same record at the same time (record contention conflict) possibly using the same logicware. For example interactive telecommunications terminals. c. the possibility of multiple programs (possibly unaware of each others existence) contending for records at the same time. The importance of this characteristic is that a logical bug in one of the programs may create data errors in the data base for which the other programs are unprepared and unaware of (data base poisoning). illustrations.ocrText: Sub-file design techniques In data bases there exist a number of sub-files. These may be classified by the record types they contain, or by the activity degree which the records show or by any arbitrary criteria of interest to the designer, such as which programs or users access, or have legal access to the sub-files. There is a need for design techniques which make a distinction between sub-files so that they may be clearly and simply distinguished by program logic and so that avoidable interaction does not occur. Undesireable interaction between subfiles may be: a. overhead costs in space-time and co-ordination of common resource use. b. reliability problems (attempt to change a record in one sub-file destroys part of another sub-file) by accident. c. security problems: ability to read or modify one sub-file is limited in relation to the others. There must be reasonable protection against intentional misuse of the file. The basic techniques fall into two distinct categories: a. logical separation: using dataware structures to allow logicware to distinguish between sub-files. b. physical separation: data base partitioning or data base modularization. illustrations.ocrText: Technique: Data base modularization Also called data base partitioning, reverse dumping. No really well established term is commonly used for this technique. DESCRIPTION The data base is resident on a master data base which is normally used in a read only mode in order to extract sub-sets of the master. Updating may be carried out temporarily to sub-data bases, and later in a more permanent manner to the master data base. Sub-data bases cannot communicate with or affect each other directly. They must do so via changes to the master data base. An exception to this would be if a "common" temporary update file were used by several sub-data bases. The left diagram shows how traditional dumping perpetuates errors (marked with 'x') from the working database through backup copies. The right diagram illustrates how reverse dumping (physical modularization) corrects errors automatically by refreshing the working database from
illustrations.ocrText: h. Data Base reliability is enhanced. The basic reason for this is that the working copy is the set of data that is subject to the class of attacks which occur during normal application use of the working data bases. The master data base itself is "off line". It is not directly subject to hardware errors, operating system bugs or application program errors. All of these classes of errors may destroy records being processed, and they may also destroy records which the application does not process records directly, such as "records in the same block" and records between which a new record is being linked to (in which case pointer fields, at least, will be modified). In "normal data base reliability procedures" such errors are collected during application use of the data base, and then perpetuated into data base dump copies. With data base physical modularization (reverse dumping) such errors are eliminated either during the master updating procedures, or by "refreshing" the working copy during master DB loading onto the working DB. Some errors which have occurred in records in the working DB may in fact be automatically corrected before they have had the opportunity to cause damage i

illustrations.ocrText: 1.0 Introduction Datocracy is the idea that political power can be distributed by digital data, rather than to politicians and parties. Technology is capable of 'eliminating the middle person'. The wishes of the people will be given directly to the action point. We can think of these action points in conventional terms, departments, directorates, ministries, international organizations. Any instance capable of carrying out instruction to change a law, change a plan, allocate resources, defend us, protect us, or research us; for example. We have needed the politicians, up until the present decade of history. But our technological level allows us to automate the political interface; as it has with so many other things like banking, knowledge distribution, medical services, physical travel, etc. There are some problems with politicians, their parties, their coalition governments, their powers, their corruption, their human inability to understand what people should be delivered, and their ability to actually deliver what is really needed, cost-effectively. illustrations.ocrText: Overview Stakeholders 3.0 Stakeholders Stakeholders are any entities (people, things) that exist in a defined system, and which have a set of requirements for being there, and succeeding there. Failure to satisfy even one critical requirement, for even one critical stakeholder can result in the entire system's collapse or severe damage. Ignorance of critical stakeholders and their critical needs makes it impossible to consciously satisfy their needs, and we will incur a risk of failure of some degree as a result. There are, in even simple systems, a large number of stakeholders to consider. In a Datocracy there are vast numbers to consider, thousands of which might be critical. Think of a Corona Virus as a stakeholder, and you will understand and believe me, I hope. Yes, the Corona Virus has 'needs' which governments must plan to satisfy, or we are in big trouble. Did you notice? illustrations.ocrText: How Inputs are Designed / 9 the system. The input designs must be portable. To us, the writers of a book on input design, it means that our lessons must transcend particular hardware features and touch upon deep, invariant principles of input design. For these reasons, we shall restrict our discussion of input design to the "soft" parts, and touch upon hardware only when differences in hardware might be relevant to design choices concerning "software." By software, here, we mean not so much the computer programs, but the messages themselves--the information flowing between people and computers. HOW WE GOT WHERE WE ARE TODAY It's difficult to keep hardware from creeping into input design. For one thing, we've been using hardware so long that most system designers have little idea what things were like before Herman Hollerith brought the punch card down from the mountaintop. For that reason, we want to sketch an evolution that brought us where we are today, as a prelude to some thoughts about where we will be tomorrow. From that moment, layer upon layer of machinery and procedures was added to counteract some limitation of the card unit record. In the end, the layers themselves came to be "the system" to most of us. In a typical system, why is lost in a maze of how, as in Figure 1.4, below. illustrations.ocrText: Positional Messages / 75 RECORDING OF ERRORS It's always dangerous to leave no record of what was done. A minimal requirement for any error-correcting system is an error-log. The log's job is to ensure that every error is recorded--on tape, or disk, or some other processing medium. Once the log exists, other programs can generate reports that show patterns in the errors. If there is a design flaw that induces errors, it may produce a recognizable pattern on one of these reports. For instance, we see below a portion of a report obtained by sorting error records from the log and tabulating them into categories: ITEM NAME: TRANSACTION CODE DESCRIPTION: ALPHA, POSITIONAL, VARYING TOTAL ENTRIES COVERED BY LOG = 37,412 REPORTING THRESHOLD FOR ANY ERROR = 5 CORRECT CODE KEYED AS CORRECTION PATTERN FREQUENCY IN SAMPLE RFE REF --FE 196 RFE REF --EF--FE 14 This portion of the report reveals a strong tendency to key RFE as REF. The tendency is so strong that in 14 cases, the same error was made on the first attempt at correction. ("--EF--FE" means "backspace, backspace, E, F, backspace, backspace, F, E".) illustrations.ocrText: Checkwords / 161 In this example, independence is likely to be achieved to a high degree because of such factors as: One is numeric and the other is alphabetic, so a keying or handwriting bias is unlikely to affect both in the same way. illustrations.ocrText: Musk's Methods The Purpose of this booklet I believe that it might useful if we examined Elon Musk's (August 2021 Video by Tim Dodd) '5 Processes' for developing his products (SpaceX, Tesla). There seems to be some good advice there. Musk has accomplished some impressive things. I suspect there is a danger that people might not correctly interpret what Musk is actually saying. A danger that Musk is not giving us all the details. That we do not know how Musk thinks. That lesser capacities might need more explicit specification of the ideas. That the ideas might be missing some critical ideas that Musk actually assumes we would know he is implying. I also suspect that we can add to these ideas for certain purposes and environments. Both, add to the detail, and add to the set of ideas. I recognize the ideas as similar and related to my own Planguage ideas (Gilb, Competitive Engineering, 2005) and so it is tempting to compare the ideas, and map similarities and differences. https://www.gilb.com/p/competitive-engineering (free pdf) TOM GILB COMPETITIVE ENGINEERING A HANDBOOK FOR SYSTEMS, REQUIREMENTS AND SOFTWARE ENGINEERING MANAGEMENT USING PLANGUAGE Page 6 of 166 Musk's Methods

illustrations.ocrText: Measure Measured Metrics 1.7 When measurement methods are meaningful. Measurement pays off, .... sometimes. Quantification is extremely useful for communicating ideas about variables, like values, qualities and costs. In early planning stages you might need to quantify, but you do not yet need to measure what happens in reality. Measurement comes in to play when you are actually delivering an increment of your strategies to the real system, and you want to get more accurate feedback, than just the smile on the face of a user. For many increment-delivery situations, you do not need to measure. And for many measuring situations you do not need to measure extremely accurately - which can save you a lot of time and effort. Sometimes the 'user smiles' are excellent feedback, and potentially more-meaningful than some measurements. There is the general principle that if pays off to discover problems as early as 'user smiles'. My preferred variation of this is Dynamic Design to Cost, where we chip away incrementally at costs, in a series of steps, over time. This is clearly Musk's Method. He is very conscious of it. He uses every incremental cycle, for example a week of Tesla production, or a cycle of SpaceX liftoffs, to motivate and support his teams, to both improve qualities, like Safety, and at the same time - reduce costs (of production, purchase, component-construction, or rocket fuel, for example). There is no excuse for putting off the act of saving cost. Company bureaucracy tries not to stop you, and it tries to make sure you have authority, money, fearlessness, and motivation to 'just do it - now, today, this cycle'. The 27-average-changes to Tesla production, per week are partly to improve car quality, but also to improve production costs, post-sale claim levels, and component costs. illustrations.ocrText: Design to Cost $120,000 / $3,000 = 30.8 x cost improvement BY DESIGN Journalist Ashlee Vance gives a colorful example of how Musk does it in his 2015 biography of Musk. In 2004, SpaceX needed a part called an actuator for its first rocket, the Falcon 1, and Musk tasked engineer Steve Davis to build it. Vance describes what happened next: Davis had never built a piece of hardware before in his life and naturally went out to find some suppliers who could make an electro-mechanical actuator for him. He got a quote back for $120,000. "Elon laughed," Davis said. "He said, 'That part is no more complicated than a garage door opener. Your budget is five thousand dollars. Go make it work.'" Davis spent nine months building the actuator. At the end of the process, he toiled for three hours writing an email to Musk covering the pros and cons of the device. The email went into gory detail about how Davis had designed the part, why he had made various choices, and what its cost would be. As he pressed send, Davis felt anxiety surge through his body knowing that he'd given his all for almost a year to do something an engineer at another aerospace company would not even attempt. illustrations.ocrText: Design to Cost Motivate continuous cost reduction everywhere Many planners try to answer the question 'how much will it cost?'. It is an interesting question, of course. But it is the wrong question. Musk's question is, for a given thing: can we radically, and competitively, reduce the costs, compared to others, incrementally, in the long term. Maybe by an order of magnitude? By using creative imaginative design engineering. Can we engineer ways to stay within tight restrictions of costs (don't use the term 'budget' in front of him!) So that we can sell more, and earn more, and compete more. This is what I call Dynamic Design To Cost. It is not a once-off design effort. It is a long-term, many-iteration continuous process. Not for 'next years model', but for next week's production if possible, even just a little improvement. Keep moving forward. Keep experimenting. Look for new-tech breakthroughs. Get rid of some robots and use humans, (Model-3 Production) if that is the answer. illustrations.ocrText: Communication and Meeting Rules: Logical and Directly Musk has a handful of oddly specific, 'unwritten' rules for his employees at Tesla, though it's hard to deny that they've played a major role in his success. The rules (from Musk's 2018 Email to employees), as detailed by Your Tango, often pertain to meetings, productivity and the free flow of information. As far as big meetings go, Musk believes that they're largely a waste of time and that they should be infrequent. Additionally, he has said that employees should "walk out of a meeting or drop off a call as it is obvious you aren't adding value," adding that he doesn't think it's "rude to leave," but rather "it is rude to make someone stay and waste their time." The way employees spend their time is of deep value to Musk, as someone who focuses so heavily on efficiency. He also believes in following "logic, not rules," emphasizing the fact that company rules may not apply in every situation, and that it's best to do what makes sense. illustrations.ocrText: Modularity A key method to scaling "But when Elon Musk announced that Tesla would build Gigafactory 1 (today known as Giga Nevada), the world's largest factory by footprint, he envisioned it in modular terms. His Lego was a small factory. Build one, get it working. Build another beside it and integrate the two. Build a third, a fourth, and so on. By building Gigafactory 1 this way, Tesla started turning out batteries and earning revenue within a year of the announcement, even as work continued on the whole giant facility, which will consist of twenty-one "Lego blocks" when completed." The key elements of modularity appear to be central to Elon Musk's general approach to engineering, and he uses them in remarkably different ventures. Tesla would seem to have nothing to do with SpaceX, a Musk creation that is revolutionizing space transport and services. But the use of replicability to shoot up the learning curve, accelerate delivery, and improve performance is woven into the company's planning and delivery model. Phrase Analysis: sentences and statements The purpose of phrase analysis Is to identify and separate significantly different types of specification (an Objective like those in Fig. 2.0 is a phrase). So that they can get necessary respectful treatment, specification and evaluation Unfortunately, it is common practice to mix together, even in one sentence, several very different types of planning object. For example 'Objectives + Strategies + Background Info'. They 'phrases' need to be separated, so that they can be properly specified, and then later 'linked together', to show their relationships. If we allow this customary 'sloppy mixture' of very different planning elements to persist, it will destroy the effectiveness of our plans. We will not get well-defined and clear objectives. We will be burdened with the wrong strategies, because they were 'born prematurely', and selected without respect to many other concurrent requirements. Here are some very specific examples of core, background, and 'administrative background' parameters to describe a Plan Object, like an objective. In this case these are concepts defined in Planguage [B1] and in the 700+ item Planguage Glossary [P4]. The Core is the set of ideas for the main planning object itself, the requirement, the design, the stakeholder. The Background is everything else, non-core. Things about the past, history, older versions of the plan, suggestions that are not yet the official plan, minority opinions, defects found lists, review reports, relationships to everything especially stakeholders, and to other Plan Objects like Objectives and Strategies, and Contracts. Finally we can distinguish a set of Background specs which are not related to the plan object idea itself (the requirement, the strategy) but are all about the administration of the Plan Object Core&Background. "I got ahold of this 'highly-secret' vision statement, and was asked to give my take on it. The background was a previously-failed large government project, and the desire to 'get it right this time'. Of course the statement is so unclear that no secrets are revealed. It is as good as 'encrypted'. My initial analysis (Fig. 3.2.6 B), was an insight into why the project was having trouble.The usual lack of clarity of objectives and strategies. I secretly and remotely helped to analyse the statement. I will attempt a reproduction of what I did, using 'Planalysis', so as to bring out the principles and consequences. There must be dozens of such projects in every nation, right now. Wouldn't it be nice if they were clear, as opposed to 'unclear'? If I were the enemy of these nations, there is hardly any simpler and cheaper strategy to make these projects worthless, than to inject such 'Visions' as the core of the project. In fact, maybe that is exactly what happened, and the traitors should be identified and rendered ineffectual?

Project requirements can be thought of as three things: functional requirements, quality requirements, and budget requirements (or resource limitations). ■ 3.6 Attribute requirements The difficult management problem centers around the 'how well' requirements. I call this area the attribute specification. Attributes are of two kinds: resources and qualities or benefits. Resources (people, time, money) are almost always limited. Resource attributes are constraints or limits on our ability to get the qualities we want. We suffer when we don't have enough quality (Figure 3.2). I find that people are pretty good at stating their resource limitations: 'I want it finished by 1 January. In a typical management situation it is almost impossible to state a set of goals for anything without • getting a list of many goals instead of one or two; • finding that any and every goal is in some kind of conflict with one or more of the others; • realizing that, quite simply, some goals are more important than others, and this makes sorting out conflicts between goals even more difficult. The comparative analysis of complex alternatives is therefore a very common problem in management decision making. The solution comparison method is designed to help resolve this problem - to enable us to choose the 'best' option from among a number of apparently satisfactory ones. It is all the non-hardware components of a system which need the attention of engineering and management. ■ Introduction It is the purpose of this chapter to remind us of our sins, at least those I see professionals regularly committing in their workplace. I do not intend to repeat the conventional wisdoms of programming, such as structures, proofs, and high-level languages. Neither do I intend to repeat, at length, ideas which apply, but which I have covered elsewhere. Briefly: software must be conceived of as something far broader than program code. From a technical system design point of view, there may be little or no difference between maintainability and improvability. Has it been altered by persons or by accident, or has it been tapped for information (which is now less secret than supposed)? illustrations.ocrText: 374 Software engineering management Resources Time  People  Money  Tools  Other resources Figure 19.9 Limited resources. Practical hint: Don't be too concerned with defining the attribute category itself. The important thing is to get a specification somewhere of all critical attributes. People This measure covers all people-related resources such as 'work years' to construct a system, and people needed to staff or operate it. These serve as limiting objectives or 'constraints' when designing a system, and when controlling its resource consumption in operation. If a goal was set that a system would only require one human clerk operator per terminal per day, and in practice it required two (because of legal regulations concerning continuous hours sitting on a terminal) then there is some evidence of a design error - and perhaps the need for redesign of the system. If fifteen people are needed to produce a system and only five are available, the development is resource limited. Money This covers all types of monetary costs of building and maintaining the system. 'Maintenance cost' would fit in here, even though maintainability is also specified as a quality. Money is a budget limit.

ATPs cover module tests done by coders on their own work. Table 21.5 below shows the impact of inspections on four ATPs. The original plans contained descriptions of 66 tests, each test consisting of one or more test cases. After inspection, only 34 of these tests remained unchanged, i.e. error free; 10 had been clarified (minor changes), 22 had been enhanced (further test cases added) and 26 totally new tests had been added. It was estimated that the resulting increase in test coverage was about 57%. The main areas affected were regression and performance testing. For the record, the four inspections cost 43 hours and resulted in 18 hours of rework;

The results were astounding. Altogether 168 major defects were found at a cost of 94 hours. A further 105 hours were spent in rework. As defect removal processes, such as inspection, are unlikely to be more than 70% effective, it was likely that at least 70 major defects remained. By now, however, most of the projects were well into the coding phase, so there seemed little point in re-inspecting the requirements. illustrations.ocrText: 3.1.0 Stakeholder Engineering [5, SE] Where does the 'Productivity Stream' go to, and where do we fund the Values? The well-developed 'Stakeholder' concept is useful for understanding Productivity in any system, because: 1. FIND THEM: If you miss out on (do not find, do not analyze, do not understand their Values and Resources, and constraints), then you will fail to get their stakeholder resources, to get their support, and you might fail to realize that you must deliver Values to particular stakeholders. 2. POWER: Stakeholders have power. Legal power, influence, money, public support, votes, and many more types of power. If you effectively ignore them, they will either opt out of your system (not buy, not support), opt into an enemy or competitor system. Or they will take active measures to punish you: strike, go slow, fake news, fine you, sue you. 3. ENEMIES: stakeholders are not all friendly, or potential customers, users, or allies. Some are competitors, some are jealous enemies, some are hackers, some want to destroy you and your organization, for bad selfish reasons. illustrations.ocrText: 3.3.2 Efficiency: Values:Costs, are impacted by choice of 'Design' The common poor practices, that threaten real 'systems efficiency (Productivity)' 1. ISOLATED VALUES: Discussing (presenting, evaluating, approving) one single value idea (like: comfort, addictiveness, usability, security) without simultaneously documenting the other critical values in the same set of values, for the project, or improvement process. 2. FUZZY VALUES: discussing values with nice words, rather than clear metrics. For example: 'Market Leading Safety' 3. NO DESIGN: discussing Values, without any well-specified satisfactory design (strategy, architecture, means) being on the table (in the background, but explicitly present), so that the 'viability of the Value' can be evaluated, in terms of costs and value side-effects. 4. NARROW COST THINKING: thinking of costs, only in financial terms (not time, people, reputation). And then thinking only in terms of Capital Costs but not recurrent costs, and maintenance costs, implementation costs, decommissioning costs. This is an unrealistic cost picture. Surprise: these other costs will occur! Scope Values Designs Efficiency Resources Designs carry a set of Values,

illustrations.ocrText: 4.5 Are you reasonably 'balanced'? 5. RE-BALANCING: The choice of the 'really most critical' productivity factors, to attend to, needs to be continuously reviewed, and is always a balance between different stakeholders. 1. The potential number of value and costs which we might have some stakeholders interested in improving; is a larger number of factors, than we can realistically hope to do well. You can't make everybody happy! 2. If we try to satisfy a too large a number of wishes, from our stakeholders, we will quickly run out of resources to create that improved productivity, and to maintain it. 3. The solution I know of is 'tough prioritization'. You select a few really-critical stakeholders, and a critical few of their Values, and hope to do a first-class job, with them. 4. The others, can be ignored, sometimes. But it might a good idea to satisfy them to some degree (a Tolerable level), or to promise to deal with them 'later'; especially if resources can be found 'extra' to do so. 5. I call the factors that we have to choose to deal with 'critical'. Critical stakeholders, critical Values, and critical costs. 6. We can build up our inventory of critical factors incrementally.

illustrations.ocrText: 8.0 Starting Points There are many possible starting points to improve a system's productivity. In simple terms you must identify an interesting improvement 'Value' or 'Cost', and then, identify a solution to improve it, and then deliver that solution incrementally to your system, and see if that really improves productivity, at the 'stakeholder end' of things. Ask them. Then, repeat until you have no more productivity improvement needs, or have no more resources to use to improve productivity. The Tesla Mob technique [29, Justice] is an interesting extreme. The 'self-forming' mob team, starts a 12-hour shift by setting an improvement target for the day. They then work through the problem together, including assignment rotation every 7 minutes, digital models, physical prototypes, and try to get as far as real implementation in production, or into their place in the supply chain. Another starting tactic for Productivity, is to use critical elements. Most critical stakeholder. Their most critical Value or Cost. illustrations.ocrText: 2.1 2. Main Principles and Features We will attempt a short description of the major elements of the database organization here. The object is to get an overall grasp of fundamentals before handling the same subject in somewhat more detail later. 2.1 The Primary Record Chain Record Number(ex.) 31 32 33 34 35 36 ABEL BAKER CHARLIE DOG EASY FOX 64 word = 256 CHARACTER RECORDS Fig 2 a. The Basic records are organized in ascending Alphabetical Sequence. New records are placed in available ("free") space. They are then connected to the rest of the file by means of references called POINTERS. The new added o: records are always LOGICALLY in alphabetical sequence. They are never physically in sequence. Although it is not strictly necessary before new records are added to the file (because then the next logical record is always the next physical record), we always look for the next record in logical (=alphabetical) sequence by means of the pointer word. The pointer word is the last word (24 bits or 4 characters) in the 64 word (256 characters) record. It contains a binary number which is equal to its relative record number in the file. illustrations.ocrText: 2.3 ALPHA INDEX 2.3 The Alphabetic Index BACKGROUND Naturally we can find any record in the file ("the file" = our data base) by searching from first to last record using the pointers to give us a correct logical sequence. To save some time when looking for "ZAMUCK" we could begin towards the end. In fact we could pretty quickly (in 8 to 20 seek-and-examine record operations) localize the desired record using a method known as "binary search" which systematically and repeatedly (using the fact of sequence of the records) halves the file and determines which side the record must be in until only one record remains. illustrations.ocrText: 4.1 continues Jacks shop ──→ JOINS BOOKSHOP ──→ ← main customer record ⌊INV 23 PAY 69 BAL 21─┐ │detailed quarterly billing CRED 10               │information Fig 4.1b: customer account chain example 4.1 d. one-time customers A "one-time" customer is one who must pay each individual invoice separately - i.e. he has no account with us and each order is treated completely separately. To simplify the process of collecting money from such customers we create a complete customer record for each new order from a one-time customer and place it in the data base. We thus have all needed information for sending reminders, calculating outstanding debts and automatically confirming or determining the source of a payment. Normally we would simply place such one-time customer records in the main chain of the data base as though we had added a new account customer with only one purchase. This would mean a severe reduction of speed in searching for books and customers on the main chain and (since book/customer searches are very frequent) thus giving an increase in machine-time and costs. Stakeholders The stakes are 'potential' requirements • Once we have agreed on some basic ideas of what we are planning for, like area, market, people, tasks: which we can call the 'Plan Scope', the 'environment', we can take a next logical planning step: identify potential stakeholders. 'Potential' means we reserve the right to exclude or to down-prioritize them later. But, we do not know enough about them, to do so - yet. • One 'tool' I use, to quickly make some planning decisions, is to use the 'priority' term 'critical'. I want to deal with the critical stakeholders first, because, by definition, if I do not, then they still might have the power to destroy my planned system. • This power can be 'legal, market, preference, economic, military': but they have that power, and have been seen to use it, or to threaten to use it, or suspected of being willing to use it - if we are not 'nice enough' to them. [SE]. 'Nice enough' means 'delivering values to at least Tolerable levels'. • Many methods of planning are doomed to fail, because they have too narrow an idea of 'stakeholders' [SE]. illustrations.ocrText: 2.2.5 The next most-effective Threat Reduction Objectives Danger Threat Attack Prevention Attack Built-in Defense Gross Damage Post-Damage Mitigation Net Damage Danger Pathway Threat To achieve 50% threat reduction, we would need approximately 3-4 well-crafted objectives focusing on the most critical threat vectors. To achieve 99% threat reduction, we would likely need to specify 15-20 different objectives, covering a wide range of threat entities, real attacks, attacked systems, and prevention strategies. This higher number is necessary to address the long tail of less common but still significant threats, as well as to provide comprehensive coverage across all aspects of military communication networks and systems. It's important to note that these estimates are approximate and would vary based on the specific military context, current threat landscape, and the comprehensiveness of each objective's prevention strategies.

illustrations.ocrText: 2.8 Post-Damage Mitigation (PDM) Post-Damage Mitigation Introduction to Post-Damage Mitigation (PDM). 1. PDM, or 'disaster cleanup' as the Red Cross calls it, is what we can do, in order to reduce the initial damage done by the attacks; the 'Gross Damage'. 2. We can do nothing, and then 'just suffer' the Gross Damage. But usually there are strategies that we can invest in, in advance, or even after the attack, to reduce the total (Gross, Initial) damage, or its effects. Rebuilding a home with a fire insurance payout, is a simple example of this. But, do not imagine you can get the fire insurance, after your home is burned down. Up-front investment is generally necessary, by someone, even if it is 'the government', 'not the citizen'. 3. If we could actually prevent any attacks from ever happening, then there would be no Damage, and no need for PDM. As the old saying goes, "An ounce of Prevention is worth a Pound of Cure" (16:1 ratio). Not smoking beats cancer cures and operations, or worse outcomes. 4. illustrations.ocrText: 3.0    Cost Engineering A tactic for handling uncertainty, threats, attacks and damages • [Cost Engineering] is a discipline we can learn and apply to the book's main theme, or dealing with uncertainty, threats, attacks, and damage to our system. 'Cost Engineering' is my book about this discipline in detail. • This is a discipline using engineering design methods, to manage any types of cost (money, people, time, space, resources) at any time, by 'design'. 'Design' meaning 'by changing the specific architecture, design, means - as well as changing the many value and cost requirements', so that we get better 'balance of values and costs. For example reducing an availability requirement from 99.998% to 99.90 might reduce costs by at least 10x. • This cost engineering is something we should use throughout the system lifecycle. illustrations.ocrText: 5.4 What is a 'design'? It is the key thing we can choose for meeting requirements. Design strategies determine all your costs • Each specific detailed design, as implemented, carries with it a set of costs. • You cannot, normally, delete or adjust the costs you do not like. • They are hardwired into that specific design, at the moment it is integrated into your system. • All you can do is to change the design, to another design, with a better set of costs. • You can analyze, present, and view, designs of alternative and similar nature, but each with different cost sets, using an Impact Estimation Table, and select the best option you have estimated. A 'design' is chosen because it gives good Value impacts and low Costs What is Design? A design is a suggested solution to the problem specified by the design requirements. It might not turn out to be valid, or as efficient as alternative solutions. A 'perfect', valid, design specification set would • deliver 'all value requirement levels' within their deadlines • While not exceeding any 'resource budgets' • And not exceeding 'any other specified constraints' PERFECT DESIGN Cost extent Less cost More value PERFECT DESIGN Value Impact T

illustrations.ocrText: 3.15 Managing Multiple Costs at Once The main point here is that we cannot oversimplify, by focussing on a single cost. If we do, we risk solving one cost problem, and creating unknown other- types-of-cost-problems. The dominating cost, during a system life-cycle, is usually the operational cost, which can easily become more than 10X the capital cost. Software people call this 'Technical Debt'. Immature short-term management, routinely allows organizations to totally ignore planning, and designing in, low operational costs (OpEx), in favor of the almighty capital budget. Mature disciplines, such as aircraft, have learned to balance these costs. Software has not. illustrations.ocrText: 3.17 The Penta Model A slightly more detailed definition. [Penta] 1. Scope: is the specified set of stakeholder- and system- functions (what it must do) and constraints (what it must not do). Scope draws a 'Does' border around a given system. 2. Values: is the specified set of stakeholder values ('wants', 'needs', 'wishes', 'visions') and system qualities, including system performance attributes ('potential values' for stakeholders). 3. Efficiency: is 'effectiveness-to-costs ratio'. Effectiveness includes all stakeholder-values actually delivered. The costs are life-cycle costs, not just 'capital' costs. This is a view outside the black box of Designs. 4. Resources: are any critical and prioritized, set of limited resources [Resource Budgets], for the system lifecycle, such as time, money, people, space. 'Costs' are the 'actual or planned' consumption of available Resources. 5. Designs: are any types of 'implementable ideas' (designs, strategies, architecture, solutions) which we use, in order to deliver Values, within Constraints and Budget limits. illustrations.ocrText: 3.20. Impact Estimation Principles One way to learn and view the IET Tool Principles: Impact Estimation [CE] 2005. 1. The Principle of 'Words being difficult to weigh' Non-numeric estimates of impact are difficult to analyze and improve upon. A design idea described as 'excellent' could actually be worse than another merely described as 'good.' 2. The Principle of 'Doubtful digits are better than none' A bad numeric estimate, and its definition, can still be systematically criticized and improved. In fact, a random number is a better starting estimate than flowery, descriptive words. 3. The 'Evident' Principle Estimates without sources, evidence, and credibility are not evident. 4. The Principle of 'Uncertainty in no uncertain terms' The uncertainty estimate is at least as important as the main estimate. 5. The Principle of the 'Seat Belt' A safety margin is as necessary with uncertain estimates, as a seat belt is with uncertain traffic. 6. How do I relate the pursuit of system efficiency, to managing the handling of attacks, uncertainties and problems, in the main priority pursuit of stakeholder value? illustrations.ocrText: 'Scale' Principles A deeper understanding of how to use Scales © Tom Gilb 081225 1. DEFINITION: Scale defines the units of measure 2. ALIGNMENT: Scale aligns project development and operations people to the same understanding of a Scale of measure 3. MANY: Many Scale definitions are possible 4. STAKEHOLDER: The best definitions of Scale will align with your critical stakeholder needs, very well. 5. SET: Sometimes, a set of Scales, will give the most-useful definition of a value. (See next following pages for examples) 6. HARMFUL: A bad, or irrelevant, Scale - can do more harm, than good. 7. RELATION: The point of a Scale - is not to measure, but it is to relate to stakeholder values. 8. IMPROVE: We can improve a Scale definition, for many reasons, like experience, regulation, available measures, social comfort, and refinement. 10. QUALITIES: The qualities of Scales, like relevance, intelligibility, familiarity, impact) for a given purpose, determine the potential quality of systems engineering, and success. illustrations.ocrText: What is the advantage of separating 'Scale' as a Planguage parameter? Our usual habit is to integrate the scale in a statement, Like 'The 5G is 100 MB/second' 1. REUSE Globally: The Scale is used in many different system or project or organizational contexts, and people immediately know, from training and experience, what it means. 3. LEARNING: once people have experience using a Scale, they know the possible and probable consequences, for example in designs, or for costs, from experience. 4. CRAFTING: once we know that the Scale is a one-time event, we do not mind crafting it to be precise or otherwise better, even if it is longer. 5. illustrations.ocrText: 'Scale' the most critical aspect. [Scale] 2026 2.2 Scales and Measures Across Aspects The interesting 'aspect' of a Scale of measure aspect, is that Planquage defines a Scale as the default base for very many other aspects. [Scale] A well-defined (clear, relevant) Scale has a multiplier-effect. All other related aspects benefit from its qualities. This applies, of course, to the Value definition aspects, like Ambition, Meter, Benchmarks (Past, Status, Ideal], Scale Constraints, like Tolerable, Targets (Wish, Goal, Stretch, Monster, Trigger). The whole set of 'parameter' aspects. The understanding of a stakeholder, is in terms of 'stakeholders' critical needs'. These needs, in turn, are ultimately defined by a Scale of measure. Even though we might start the process of defining their needs, by informal terms, such as those used by the stakeholders ('more flexible', 'easy to repair'); we, for serious large-scale, complex, systems - need to define, a relevant and clear Scale of measure, with which to 'manage' the stakeholder understanding and stakeholder expectations. illustrations.ocrText: Height and Length https://x.com/MediocreJoker85/status/2001302617490927972?s=20 Two engineers were standing at the base of a flagpole, craning their necks and squinting up at the top. They paced around it, pointed, argued quietly, and scratched notes on a clipboard. A woman walking by slowed down and asked, "What are you two doing?" "We're supposed to find the height of this flagpole," one engineer explained, "but we don't have a ladder, a drone, or anything tall enough to measure it." The woman shrugged, reached into her purse, pulled out a wrench, and loosened a couple of bolts at the base. The flagpole gently tipped over and landed flat on the ground. She then took a tape measure from her pocketbook, stretched it from one end to the other, and said, "Twenty-one feet, six inches." She put her tools away, calmly walked off down the path, and continued on her way. One engineer stared after her for a moment, then shook his head and laughed. "Well, that doesn't help us at all. We asked for the height... and she gave us the length." LaughBreak: Dad Jokes 'N More @MediocreJoker85 Grok Version 4.1 Video

PDM, or 'disaster cleanup' as the Red Cross calls it, is what we can do, in order to reduce the initial damage done by the attacks; the 'Gross Damage'. 2. We can do nothing, and then 'just suffer' the Gross Damage. But usually there are strategies that we can invest in, in advance, or even after the attack, to reduce the total (Gross, Initial) damage, or its effects. Rebuilding a home with a fire insurance payout, is a simple example of this. But, do not imagine you can get the fire insurance, after your home is burned down. Up-front investment is generally necessary, by someone, even if it is 'the government', 'not the citizen'. 3. If we could actually prevent any attacks from ever happening, then there would be no Damage, and no need for PDM. illustrations.ocrText: 3.1 Resources The limited fuel to pay for value results Resource               Concept *199 May 19, 2003 A resource is any potential system input. A resource is any kind of input 'fuel' necessary for building, operating or maintaining a given system. A resource is an asset or a supply that can be used to produce the functionality, or performance levels, of a system. A resource can be defined using a scale of measure. A requirement, for a resource, can be specified by a target level, or a constraint level. Previous levels of resource utilization (incurred costs) can be specified by benchmark levels, like Past. We can distinguish between budgeted and unbudgeted resources. Resource budgets are found in our formal plans. But, although a small project might actually have such a volume of stakeholders, even a single human does. Here is a useful simplification. Agree on your top-ten stakeholders, listed on a single page. Make sure you go well beyond the usual 'user and customer' stakeholders, and include suppliers, contracts, laws, and competitors. This will force you to be conscious of some 'too costly' stakeholders! See Chapter 2, Stakeholders. 2. REQUIREMENTS: [VR] Then (after Stakeholders) analyze just the top-ten stakeholders, to find the most critical requirement for each one of them. The top 10 requirements. And simplify each one, to 'Tag/Scale|Goal'. That at least, makes you to quantify the critical Value requirements. This will make you to sense that some of your most ambitious Goal levels can be too costly. This includes specific 'cost reduction' requirements. See Chapter 3, Values. 3. SOLUTIONS: For each Requirement
