illustrations.ocrText: 5.2 Some Basic Stakeholder Principles STAKEHOLDER PRINCIPLES. (© gilb.com 2020, Governeering book) 1. Some stakeholders are more critical to your system than others. 2. Some stakeholder needs are more critical to your system than others. 3. Stakeholders are undisciplined: they may not know all their needs, or know them precisely, or know their value. But they can be analyzed, coached, and helped to get the best possible deal. 4. Stakeholders may be inaccessible, unwilling, inanimate, oppositional, and worse: but we need to deal with them intelligently. 5. Stakeholders might well ask for the wrong thing, a 'means' rather than their real 'ends'. But they can be guided to understand that. Or their requests can be interpreted in their own, real, best interests. 6. Stakeholders do not want to wait years, get delays, invest shitloads of money, and then get little or no value. They want as much 'value improvement' of their current situation, as they can get, as fast as they can get it. For as little cost as possible, 7. Stakeholders cannot have any realistic idea of what their needs and demands will cost to satisfy. So their adopted (by you) requirements need to be based on value for cost

[DL]. • The most common planning fault, is to work on the 'means' - before we have clarified the 'ends' - which those means will support. • For example the term 'strategic planning' is missing emphasis on the main points. • The main point is delivering values to the stakeholders. Is it possible to agree on that simple planning-foundational idea? • I prefer to call it 'Value Planning' [Value Planning]. Were I to be even logically stricter with myself, I should probably call it 'Stakeholder Satisfaction' planning [SE]. Stakeholders The stakes are 'potential' requirements • Once we have agreed on some basic ideas of what we are planning for, like area, market, people, tasks: which we can call the 'Plan Scope', the 'environment', we can take a next logical planning step: identify potential stakeholders. 'Potential' means we reserve the right to exclude or to down-prioritize them later. But, we do not know enough about them, to do so - yet. • One 'tool' I use, to quickly make some planning decisions, is to use the 'priority' term 'critical'. I want to deal with the critical stakeholders first, because, by definition, if I do not, then they have the power to destroy my planned system. • This power can be legal, market, preference, economic, military: but they have that power, and have been seen to use it, or to threaten to use it, or suspected of being willing to use it - if we are not 'nice enough' to them. [SE] • Many methods of planning are doomed to fail, because they have too narrow an idea of 'stakeholders'. illustrations.ocrText: 9.2.2.2. Stakeholders The stakes are 'potential' requirements • Stakeholders, by definition, have their 'values'. Things they care about to some degree. These values can be articulated as 'potential' requirements. • They are of two general types: 'Performance Values' (how good the system is for them, [Value Planning]). And Constraints, limits to what they will tolerate. • If you miss a critical stakeholder, or if you miss one of their critical values; then you are far-less likely to satisfy the critical value. Guess what? Failure to deliver the 'unknown value' is probable. • So, it is worth some discipline in identifying stakeholders. It might only take an hour!. illustrations.ocrText: 10.4.2.3 Two different types of 'strategy decomposition' Evo-steps versus Tasks A large-cost strategy (it takes a month-to-years) can be decomposed in two ways: 1. Task Decomposition • This lists the many tasks which need doing, before we can expect the strategy to deliver value. • Probably no task alone delivers much value. Most tasks do not deliver the planned Value Objective Improvement towards its Goal. • Running a marathon does not deliver value until you cross the finish line, if you finish at all. 2. Sub-strategy decomposition, into Evo-steps. • This decomposes a strategy into a number of independently implementable sub-strategies, which can be implemented, in any sequence, and will each deliver value. • They can be implemented in parallel, too • These are Evo Steps; resulting in value. • A strategy can potentially be decomposed into Evo-steps. illustrations.ocrText: 10.11 Decomposition Methods The basic need and basic idea of an Evo-step decomposition • When a strategy is bigger than your Evo-step length (for example, a week step). • You need to decompose strategies into sub-strategies, no larger than your Evo-step length. • The main decomposition rule is that Evo-steps must deliver 'planned value-requirement increases', not be mere 'tasks'. • A secondary rule, though not so critical, is that the sub-strategies can be delivered in any sequence, independently of each other. Useful, for optimization, but not critical. • AI apps can do this decomposition if you ask (as in 10.4.4) • Value Evo-steps can more-easily be found, if you know the domain well. illustrations.ocrText: 10.17 The Backroom and Frontroom Here is one of the 'tricks' of decomposition: when it seems impossible. Frequently, we encounter a strategy or architecture that just refuses to divide up into our desired smaller Evo-steps of a week or so. For example a supply chain delay. I do like to say that 'everything can be decomposed, into Evo Steps'. But a birth cycle does take about 9 months, even if you try to use 9 women in parallel. The solution is to accept defeat, gracefully. With a wry smile. Some things cannot really be decomposed into weekly incremental delivery steps. But what we can do is to start the Develop stage (Evo Cycle), and the, 'wait' until it is complete enough to 'Deliver'. We put the Developing Strategy in the 'Backroom' until it is ready to Deliver. And we find something else which is actually ready to deliver, that week. Maybe even something, a 'ready to Deliver step' strategy, that has been hibernating in the Backroom until now. So, in order to more boldly make a claim to decomposition powers, it needs 'clarification'. illustrations.ocrText: 11.2.6.0 Entry Process (E), and Mirror X-Process The Entry Process, to a 'Process of Interest' (POI) is like a moat, guard, and gate to a castle or fort The E-Process intent is to make sure ('probable') that the necessary conditions for success ('Exit' succeeds) of the Process of Interest (POI), are a reality, and are 'good enough'. The E-Process idea is that it is a small-%, of a full POI work process. It is more efficient to 'fail the Entry Process,' than failing the more-costly POI. Entry Processes can be done by one person, or a computer app, or AI. The POI main task is probably done by a team of people, working for a much longer duration, than an E-Process. The 'E' (entry) process is also a device for teaching people the organizational expectations, and reminding them of the expectations, and making those expectations 'official', shared, work requirements The 'E' process is basically, 1. Check the E-Conditions. 2. Fix failed conditions if possible, 3. Fail entry to the Task of Conditions fail, and are not yet fixed. illustrations.ocrText: 3.8 How 'efficient' are the solutions An 'engineering' prioritization tactic • It is generally a good tactic to not try to deliver all strategies at once, by the deadline. That is known as the 'Waterfall Model'. Big Bang. • It is generally possible to deliver one, or a few, solutions early. • The selection, of which ones to start off with, can advantageously be made, based on the efficiency of the solution. • Efficiency is the ratio of Value/Cost, sometimes called 'cost-effectiveness'. Sometimes called 'profit'. • This allows us to focus our limited attention, and skilled people, more narrowly, and more practically: on 'getting real value', and learning (weekly, monthly), rather than 'planning' and 'developing' for a whole year. Before you find out that key solutions, do not work well, at all. • 'Exact estimation' of values and costs, is not necessary. • AI estimation will be good enough. Most of the efficient solutions, will still be in the early value delivery cycles, and most-importantly, we can focus on the 10% of the strategies initially, get some value early; and learn quickly; if we have problems that apply to the next solution delivery steps. illustrations.ocrText: 17.0 Is there a "magic calculator"? Perhaps the 'Impact Estimation Table' [VIET] will serve the purpose? First let me say that 'The Crux' (I am am on page 195 (opposite quote) of 309) is by far, the best book of the many I have read, on strategy. Both for 'theory' and for practical case studies. I have to highlight a handful of statements and ideas per page! Buy it, Read it! So, let no-one my praise and admiration for Richard Rumelt's sage advice, and useful history. But, he also challenges me to proffer answers to some questions (Chapters 15, 16). And this is another such occasion. I think my 'Impact Estimation Table' (IET) might to some degree, if not perfectly, but far better than nothing, satisfy the 'Magic Strategy Analyzer' problem. I did offer 'Impact Estimation' to Harvard Business Review, about the 1970s, but Editor Rosabeth Moss Kanter, turned it down. Maybe because I was not a professor at Harvard, or as I have later learned, I did not have an 'agent' to help me get it accepted. Probably because I presented it poorly. illustrations.ocrText: 17.1.1 Overview and Introduction Multi-dimensional thinking Value Impact Estimation (VIE) is a free, open source, method, developed by this author during his six decades of professional practice (1960-2022, now retired but active). The original inspiration was Dr. Barry Boehm's, 'Requirements-Properties Matrix' (see diagram bottom right), TRW Systems, which I (and Kai Gilb, later) evolved many improvements, to the initial idea. [SM, 1976]. I did an annual trip to TRW to present the progress. Barry wrote the foreword to [PoSEM]. The general purpose of VIE, and one 'format' of the method, the Impact Estimation Table (IET), is to help evaluate any type of 'solutions' (like strategies, tactics, designs, architecture, sub-objectives) in relation to a set of stakeholder values and resource constraints. Another conclusion from this, is that IET/VIE is 'fractal', and works at any level of concern, including the top level. Put more simply, VIE is a tool to help us better understand potential solutions to future values/costs objectives. Not, as we shall discuss, to predict the impacts of strategies, and strategy objectives; but to get some idea, rather than none, of the 'order of magnitude',

In practice we would find that drawing solution/value relationships, with lines or arrows, is clumsy, when we are dealing with many values and solutions, as we normally must do. A rats nest of lines would result. The norm in this book is that we will specify multiple relationships between multiple requirements ('ends') and their multiple solutions ('means') using a table. A tool, like [ValPlan] can draw some lines, based on the relationships in the table, when we want that visualization. We will usually be computing simple numeric sums, from the table estimates. So a simple spreadsheet might be useful. Mainly today we use a specialized app (ValPlan), and many illustrations in this Chapter, will be using that app. We are (2025) transitioning to intelligent databases [Graphmetrix.com] which can tackle relationships of anything-to-anything, and update them, for very complex systems (millions of relations), such as a large organization. illustrations.ocrText: 17.1.3.1 A Strategy Hierarchy Using Fractal Strategy Patterns "work backwards from broad goals to strategy" (Rumelt) • It would be illogical to derive top-level corporate objectives by simply 'declaring' them to be an effect (result), of all other objectives, and their strategies, at lower levels. • Although, if no strategy action is taken at the top level, the resulting status value levels, are some outcome of all strategies and effects below that level. • So, if we believe in top-down Strategic responsibility, then the top must decide and publish their official set of 'Strategy Objectives' (hypothesis). • Then, a 'plan' (of results) exists. But nothing 'real' exists, until we take some actions to change things, so that the Value Objectives actually improve. • At this point, we have some choices: • Define, design, and implement specific actions, 'strategies', or 'strategic actions'. Hoping that these will fulfill the Goal levels of your Value Objectives. • Or, design, plan, another set of second-level Strategic Objective Goals, which when achieved, will cause us to reach the Top- level objectives. • In the first case (strategy Actions) we can hope that things might improve in the

illustrations.ocrText: 17.3.8 When the 'means' is a 'Means' objective level, and is not a 'thing to do' (action) 'Means' Objectives There are two types of 'Means' to reach your 'Ends. Normally we assume we are going to find a 'Means' to 'do' (deliver to system). Some strategy/solution/design (the Rectangle icon) which, when you deliver it incrementally, to your evolving system, is estimated to improve your 'Ends' (aka requirements, qualities, value objectives (The red Arrow Symbol, for a 'variable' Value, Fig. 17.3.8 A)). In simple terms; if you want to improve a quality level you need to deliver (do) a specific quality design (means, strategy). We can not merely imagine a level, concrete action is needed to produce a value impact. However, sometimes it is necessary to deliver a subsidary, or supporting, value level, in order to achieve a higher-level critical value level (known as a 'Strategic Objective'). Of course, the 'supporting value level' (known as a 'Means Objective'), will ultimately, itself, need some specific 'Means' (a design or strategy which can be delivered incrementally, to a real system, in order to produce incremental improvement, in Value Objectives). illustrations.ocrText: 17.4.0 Value Tables: multiple values and means. Value Impact Estimation tables Up to now in this book, I have tried to carefully review the basis for Value Impact Estimation: clear requirements (VR) and clear 'means' (SEA) to reach those requirements (means or 'means objectives'). I have also tried to introduce the basic idea of estimating an impact at all. If these basic VIE components are not well-defined, well understood, and well specified, then the table itself, is a meaningless farce, like [QPD]. The basic VIE concept starts with the simple relationship (Figure 17.4.0 B) of trying to answer the question. 'How does Solution A, impact my plan to get a 'Wished' for level-of-performance, of an attribute 'A Value'. But we will never understand any strategy if we only understand a single value dimension, or single cost dimension. In any real system, even as small as your own life [Life Design] there are several highly-critical values (heart and brain, and family for example). You cannot escape the necessity of understanding the multiple impacts of a given strategy option, on all of them. The conclusion is that we must examine many values and costs, for each strategy. illustrations.ocrText: 17.4.7 Estimating ± Uncertainty Be certain of your uncertainty Nobody can predict exact future impacts in a complex system, except by pure chance. If I ask people to estimate the plus/minus uncertainty of their estimate, they can do that as a reasonable estimate, and the answer is never ±0.0 The larger the uncertainty number, the greater your risk, and the worse your 'worst case' is. Notice we can even add up the set of uncertainties for each Strategy, and get an artificial number, which tells us a little about the riskiness of the strategy, for all values and costs. This can be applied directly and numerically, as we shall discuss, to automatically computing strategy priorities, with respect to risk. We use a single ± 'normal distribution' number (±42), because this is a rough guess only. Correct order of magnitude would be nice. illustrations.ocrText: 17.4.9 The Relative Overall Value Sum In order to get some overall idea of the generic effectiveness (effectiveness on all Values) of a single Strategy (like strategy D10. Rocket from..). If we simply add up the % impacts on each Value, we get an overall number (in this case, 'Sum of Values' '32%', versus 'Elon Musk's strategy sum '139%'). It gets overwhelmingly tempting to prioritize Musk, until you see that it costs 5X more. See 'Sum of Development Resources'. Now we know that the Value Sum (32%, 139%) is just an artificial construction. But most people we work with accept it as a reasonable expression of the overall value effectiveness. It is not a perfect model of total effectiveness, but it is simple to understand and do. And it helps people see a 'set of ideas' better. Anything more complicated, like weights on each value, would entail subjective decisions (as opposed to evidence), and not necessarily give us a better practical outcome. The main purpose is pretty good prioritization, quickly, so that we get into action: creating a pretty good stream of stakeholder value. illustrations.ocrText: 17.4.12 VIE Model Accuracy Sufficient Accuracy How 'accurate' is Value Impact Estimation? The actual accuracy depends on the strategy-evidence you have. If you are dealing with bleeding-edge technology, not even on the market, and nobody you know has any experience of it: you have a problem Houston. It depends on your problems, like your ambition level targets being beyond current state of the art (nobody has any experience). We are not trying to make a perfect model or even a ±5% model. For some projects we would be happy to get the 'right order of magnitude', as engineers often are, initially, and then iteratively learn from numeric feedback, and increasing your accuracy as you scale up. What you need in estimation is accuracy, which is sufficient for purpose, and purposes vary. Accuracy does not matter much really, as long as we are open about the ± Uncertainty, and the Credibility level, based on facts. The purpose of the table is not accurate prediction. If you want better accuracy, you need to use measurement of small increments. You only need sufficient accuracy, to make smart decisions, about your strategies, and your priorities. illustrations.ocrText: 17.4.20 Value Impact Estimation Principles Principles: Impact Estimation [CE] 2005. 1. The Principle of 'Words being difficult to weigh' Non-numeric estimates of impact are difficult to analyze and improve upon. A design idea described as 'excellent' could actually be worse than another merely described as 'good.' 2. The Principle of 'Doubtful digits are better than none' A bad numeric estimate, and its definition, can still be systematically criticized and improved. In fact, a random number is a better starting estimate than flowery, descriptive words. 3. The 'Evident' Principle Estimates without sources, evidence, and credibility are not evident. 4. The Principle of 'Uncertainty in no uncertain terms' The uncertainty estimate is at least as important as the main estimate. 5. The Principle of the 'Seat Belt' A safety margin is as necessary with uncertain estimates, as a seat belt is with uncertain traffic. 6. The Principle of 'Profitable Proposals' The value of an idea is 'how well it meets objectives'. The net value considers the costs too. 7. illustrations.ocrText: 18.1 SQC Summary Spec(-ification) Quality Control [CE] SQC is the review of any product development specification type, from strategic plans to software It pays off to use SQC upstream (yes: on management planning for Products, on product requirements, before 'product design') The SQC review is always conducted with reference to the applicable 'Rules' [CE] for the Spec type. The Rules are your standards for good enough work in planning. They are all about 'clarity' and 'completeness'. To some degree, AI can do the checking work, even on a whole large document, if it has clear logical rules to work with, like 'Unambiguous, Clear to Engineers'. (See Examples in this Chapter and [CE]). AI will also produce specs according to these rules if you ask it to. But, if expensive human engineers are going to do checking, then sampling is the most cost-effective measurement process for large volume specs. The 'output of the review' is a useful estimate of the Defect Density (how badly the spec was crafted, how polluted it is, how much it will delay everything downstream and inflate costs). This Defect Density is used to 'Exit' or not. It is one Exit Condition for the Spec Process. See ETX Chap

illustrations.ocrText: 18.2 SQC Principles © Gilb 210625 19:21 1. SQC is a measurement of defect density process 2. The measured defect density is the basis for one 'Spec Exit' condition; low enough defect density 3. A defect is defined as deviation from an official 'Rule' for the Spec type. 4. There are Generic Rules (apply to many Spec Types), like 'Clarity'. And there are 'Specific Rules' which are limited to special specification types (like 'Impact Estimation' [CE]). 5. SQC is not a QC process. It is not about detecting and removing defects. It is about motivating engineers to learn, and successfully apply good practice rules, consistently. It is a Quality Assurance tactic. 6. SQC has better return on investment, the more upstream it is applied. The upstream volume is lower: the consequences of bad spec practices, on downstream work, is greater. 7. SQC can find defects better, when sufficient time-per-page is applied, like 'one hour per page' for maximum % of defects found, over 90%, this applies to humans, and is different for AI. 8. SQC is more effective with about 2-3 people, rather than 1 or 4-5. But effectiveness is not a main point, the main points are getting a realistic idea for the quality

illustrations.ocrText: 1.2 Some Basic Stakeholder Principles STAKEHOLDER PRINCIPLES. (© gilb.com 2020, Governeering book) 1. Some stakeholders are more critical to your system than others. 2. Some stakeholder needs are more critical to your system than others. 3. Stakeholders are undisciplined: they may not know all their needs, or know them precisely, or know their value. But they can be analyzed, coached, and helped to get the best possible deal. 4. Stakeholders may be inaccessible, unwilling, inanimate, oppositional, and worse: but we need to deal with them intelligently. 5. Stakeholders might well ask for the wrong thing, a 'means' rather than their real 'ends'. But they can be guided to understand that. Or their requests can be interpreted in their own, real, best interests. 6. Stakeholders do not want to wait years, get delays, invest shitloads of money, and then get little or no value. They want as much 'value improvement' of their current situation, as they can get, as fast as they can get it. For as little cost as possible, 7. Stakeholders cannot have any realistic idea of what their needs and demands will cost to satisfy. So their adopted (by you) requirements need to be based on value for cost

illustrations.ocrText: How do we figure out stakeholder requirements when they are 'inarticulate'? 4.0 Requirements Elicitation Garbage In, Goodies Out. In the next Chapter, 5, we will ask, 'do we even care to commit to deliver their 'clarified' values, or respect their constraints?' The purpose of this Chapter 4, is to figure out what the stakeholder requirements actually are, and to specify them in a clear enough manner for our evaluation, and (Ch.5) for our prioritization purposes. My observation is that most people are not trained well enough to do this. The job is rarely well done. But allow me to explain this assertion. In advanced 'stakeholder engineering' detail. illustrations.ocrText: https://tinyurl.com/PLanalysisFree 4.3.2.7 A Council Plan: The strategies I see here considerable, but unfortunately, very widespread, malpractice, of mixing up our real objectives, and suggested strategies to deliver objectives. One analysis tool, in my Planguage toolset, is to use a table, to analyze the relationship between ends and means, - i.e. between Objectives, and their servant strategies. Notice that in most examples in this book, and then also in this 'Council' example, there is no analysis of how much the suggested strategies impact any of the critical objectives. Not to mention 'how strategies impact the many budgeted resources'. The Impact Estimation Table (IET) is a big subject (B1, B2, B3, B6). It not only helps us with the analysis of objectives and strategies. It helps us with much more, including design, architecture, strategic planning, prioritization, risk management, and project result tracking. And IET has powerful mechanisms for this, which we need not get in to, here. I want to keep it simple now, and just introduce the ideas of : 1. Clear separation of ends (Objectives) and means (Strategies). 2. Analyzing the many-to-many, quantified impacts of strategies

NO RULES: There were absolutely no Rules for the specification. Things like unambiguous, complete, were ignored. 2. NO QC: There was no quality control of the specifications as handed over to the offshore supplier. This might have prevented 98% of the defects from reaching the offshore supplier. 3. These were classified as software bugs. It did not work. But they were not really 'coding errors'. They were management errors, and planning process errors. 4. illustrations.ocrText: Asking stakeholders personally 6.7 Interviews Sometimes the stakeholder analyst needs to talk to individuals or small meetings of stakeholders. Here are some considerations. Oral discussion has its place, alongside written communication. Here are some ideas about that: 1. If possible schedule meetings on their home ground, the work-site of the stakeholder. You will learn more there than in your office. 2. I had a custom of just sitting observing people at work for an hour. Things happen; like people shouting, major distractions, people cursing at a system. 3. Be clear upfront why you are there: to figure out what they need to make their work better. illustrations.ocrText: How to recognize well-performing stakeholders, and reward them. 6.11 Recognition The stakeholder recognition problem boils down to the question "How can we sense, know, measure, that a stakeholder individual, team, or organization is somehow contributing to the system, in ways that deserve formal recognition, and perhaps reward them. Some of the literature I found like [31, 32,33], was universities asking this question for their staff, in their career trajectory. I believe that we have some interesting suggested answers within the scope of this book: 'system engineering' answers, using Planguage. I can even cite one interesting case study (Confirmit, next page). The key idea I want to contribute is the one we have discussed throughout this book, particularly Chapter 4. We need to define our 'Recognition Values'. For education (or other stakeholder systems). We need to formally define, quantitatively, the critical set of values which define stakeholder performance. Then we need to collect data, or measure these values, in ongoing systems, in order to spot stakeholders, worthy of recognition. Figure 6.11 Source Tilburg [33] https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/sites/default/files/downlo

illustrations.ocrText: Recognizing Teams By Incremental Values Delivered 6.11.1 Confirmit Case of Recognition In Oslo, in 2003 we taught, 1 day, Planguage and 'Evo' (our Agile Value-Delivery method in Planguage [4] to a small 80 person company, with a product development team of 16 people, who we divided into 4 teams. A management team, a week later, produced, a Marketing-Driven set of critical product/service values quantified (see examples Figure 6.11.1). I think there were a total of 25 Values. These were divided into about 6 Values for each of the four 4-person teams. They gave the teams great freedom to figure out the necessary technical designs to reach the Value Objectives, in the coming 3 months (a quarter). The teams delivered in a weekly 'Evo' value-delivery cycle, so they could see the real values emerging on their real product 'twin', weekly. Released to customers quarterly. Notice how fast we did this. Simplified: all teams managed to deliver all Values, sometimes much more (Table 4) by the end of every quarter, for years on end. illustrations.ocrText: How to make stakeholders responsible 6.12 Responsibility Planguage [4,& SEA [22], as an engineering modeling method, has many devices for assigning very clear and specific responsibility, to various stakeholders. The basics are these: 1. Very well-defined requirements: quantified (values and costs), or testable (binary constraints, functions). Nobody can deny what was planned, agreed, was taken responsibility for, and finally achieved. 2. In addition to the 'Quantified Value requirements', we add the deadlines for them, individually (not one deadline for the whole project). So a specific requirement was for both a level of value and 'by a deadline'. 3. Specific assignment to named and defined stakeholders. Not generic stakeholders, but specific individuals or organizational units (like CTO) 4. The use of [Scale Qualifiers] and specific conditions, makes a strong case for responsibility for exactly those conditions, but nothing else. See 2nd 'Wish' Fig. 6.12 Air Quality Stakeholder Value Critical Is Part Of: Top Values Value Ambition Level: Drastically improve air quality in London to acceptable legal levels as stated in the Paris Accord (Paris Agreement) Scale: Number of [Persons]

illustrations.ocrText: Tailoring using [Scale Qualifiers]. 6.13 Tailoring to Stakeholder. illustrations.ocrText: How can we train stakeholders? 6.14 Training Principles of Stakeholder Training 1. Training can be 'by any means' that gives the particular stakeholder type, and individual, the defined competence-levels required 2. The better your definition of the 'stakeholder competence-levels', the better design of appropriate training, you can make. 3. There is generally no 'best way' to train a given stakeholder type in given skills, they vary: so, varied training designs will be most cost-effective. 4. The several required levels of performance, for stakeholders training results, can be defined, using Scales of measure, with [Scale Qualifiers] and their conditions. 5. An Impact Estimation Table can be used, to begin to understand the effectiveness, of any training design, for a set of stakeholder skills, and a set of budgeted resources. 6. You can incrementally implement sub-strategies for training, in real environments, and measure the results, before you scale up to larger groups. [Evo, 4]. See also Edu-neering [23] Example of how we can define the Values for Stakeholder Training Accountability Level: Stakeholder, Status: Not Determined Type: Value, Labels: no labels Edit Is Part Of: SHARE

illustrations.ocrText: Some useful patterns for stakeholder data collection 7.0 Stakeholder Templates Templates are basically forms to be filled out, with a structure and sequence of elements, which are suited to a defined purpose. Like collecting all known aspects about a given Stakeholder. Adam Fard, uses a series of questions (see Figure 7.0) to achieve the same purpose. These are similar to a 'checklist' (Chapter 6.2) of questions. Obstacles • Are there any technological limitations? • Are there any political, national or cultural limitations? • If we try again now, will we still hit these same obstacles? • What worries you about this project? What's the worst thing that could happen? • QA: What problems do you currently see in development? • Support or customer service: What problems do you see most often? • Training or technical documentation: Where do users most often get confused today? • What would be a reason why we would not be able to get the dream outcome? adamfard.com Stakeholder Interview Template: 120+ Questions Figure 7.0 Source: https://adamfard.com/download-ux-resources/stakeholder-interview-questions-template Page 125 of 175 Stakeholder Engineering

illustrations.ocrText: Stakeholder Patterns, Stored Wisdom 8.0 Pattern = Pattern    Concept *655  (Planguage Glossary) • A 'Pattern' is a general tool • that defines any idea structure, • or sets of structures, • in any intelligible format, • which can be exploited by tailoring it to, • or copying it into, • a specific domain. Patterns are a form of stored wisdom or knowledge. The main idea is to allow people to organize and reuse knowledge, rather than re-inventing it from scratch or memory. Examples of patterns in Planguage and the CE book are: Principles, Scales of measure, Examples, Case Studies, Processes, Procedures, Concept Glossary Definitions, Entry and Exit Rules, Rules (for Specification), Standards. Planguage as defined in Competitive Engineering is a set of diverse patterns intended to inform the user of useful structures which can either be copied or tailored to specific purposes and domains. illustrations.ocrText: Principles as Patterns 8.1 Chapter 6. Educational Content 6.3 Principles Principles of Principles 1. IMPACTFULNESS: A principle can have very strong impacts, when applied. 2. TEACHER: A principle can be used to summarize, teach, reinforce, and guide - our practice. 3. INSIGHTS: Principles are observations, of how the world functions. 4. MULTI-ATTRIBUTES: Principles have quality attributes, and cost attributes, which can guide us, as to which principles we value, and which principles we can find cost-effective to use. 5. CHANGE STRATEGIES: Principles can be used as high level strategies, for delivering improvement in organizations and processes. 6. AVOIDANCE: Principles are not universally useful, efficient, or applicable; so we need to learn or be aware of when NOT to use them. Build this into the principle. "If x..". 7. STABILITY: Principles can be used as a strategy to stabilize an educational or training syllabus, or book content. 8. CULTURE: Principles define a culture, which uses them. 9. AUTOMATION: Principles are potentially capable of automation. 10. QUOTES: Principles serve as a safe way of quoting people or knowledge. Principles for deciding if a principle is a 'keeper'.

illustrations.ocrText: Rules = Patterns for Specification 8.3 Rules R9: Clear: Specifications should be 'clear enough to test' and 'unambiguous to their intended readers.' R10: Simple: Complex specifications should be decomposed into a set of elementary, tagged specification statements. R11: Fuzzy: When any element of a specification is unclear then it shall be marked, for later clarification, by <fuzzy angle brackets>. R12: Comment: Any text which is secondary to a specification, and where no defect in it could result in a costly problem later, must be clearly identified. It can be written in italic text statements, or headed by suitable warning (such as Note, Rationale or Comment), or written in "quotes," and/or moved to footnotes. Non-commentary specification shall be in plain text. Italic can be used for emphasis of single terms in non-commentary statements. Readers should be able visually, at a glance without decoding the contents, to distinguish between 'critical' and 'non-critical' specification. STARS Conceptual Framework for Reuse Processes (CFRP) Knowledge evolves in all domains, and domain engineering methods must provide support for this evolution over time. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between incremental learning and evolution and that suggested by domain engineering. We view domain engineering as a window of parallelism within a larger evolutionary pattern that might begin with a slower building up of knowledge through cases and examples. A domain model represents a "snapshot" derived by parallel analysis of multiple instances. Once a domain model has been established the incremental process begins again, enriching or possibly "decaying" the domain model structure. Eventually, the model may need to be substantially revised; or the domain may be absorbed into boundaries of neighboring domains or due to the obsolescence of the defining technology for the domain. illustrations.ocrText: 1.1 Stakeholders Stakeholders are the entities that determine our architecture requirements for us. So we need to find a balance, in stakeholder analysis, to suit the architecture task, and a balance which pays off. illustrations.ocrText: 1.2 Values (of stakeholders) 'Values', as a concept is easily misunderstood. But it is a very useful concept. So, let us deal with it clearly. The major derailment is that people think of money value, when they hear the term value. But, we are using it in a much wider sense. We mean everything, that stakeholders value. We mean a very broad range of human values, where money is in the picture, but is not the main idea. Perhaps a simple start is the United Nations 17 Sustainable Goals [SP], like about poverty, hunger, education. Very important stuff, and it costs money. But money is not the main point. There is no simple fixed quantity of possible value statements (Value Objectives, Value Requirements) from stakeholders. Value specifications are, as we shall see (see section 10), infinite in their detail. They are whatever the stakeholder needs, and the stakeholder circumstances, are both changing, and infinitely complex. We do not give up, at this infinite value definition task. It is the basis for our architecture. We do the best we can, early. We need to do a pretty good job at capturing and prioritizing stakeholder requirements. Value is the potential consequence of system attributes, for one or more stakeholders. 2. Value is not linearly related to a system improvement: for example, a small change in an attribute level could add immense perceived value for one group of stakeholders for relatively low cost. 3. Value is the perceived usefulness, worth, utility or importance of a defined system component or system state, for defined stakeholders, under specified conditions. illustrations.ocrText: 1.5 Side Effects, a constraint, and opportunity When an architect is focussing on 'one quantified value', or quality, let us say 'Security', and trying to think about possible security architecture ideas; they can pick some ideas which seem to satisfy the Security requirements. Good start! But, then we have to ask 2 basic questions: 1. Can we afford the Security architecture? 2. What are the 'side-effects' on all other 'critical stakeholder requirements'. For example, does the architecture idea threaten 'Usability', or 'Performance Speed'? I have noticed that conventional EA methods have no real systematic approach to this. They hardly bother with any clear requirements, for a start. I could not find anything about EA and side-effects doing internet searches. Yet we all know how important side-effects are in medicines! illustrations.ocrText: 4.1 Architecture Decomposition : Reasons why we decompose Why is architecture decomposition useful? And why should the architect do it, rather than an agile project manager/ Product Owner ? Decomposition Usefulness 1. VALUE STREAM: Decomposition enables us to have an early, almost continuous value stream, of increased critical stakeholder- value, getting better, going towards targeted value levels, on time. This is essential agile, essentially avoiding big bang projects. 2. SIMPLIFICATION: Decomposition allows us to simplify large and complex systems, into a prioritized stream of small trials or experiments. 3. EARLY: Decomposition allows us to get extremely early results, this financial cycle, this election period, before the 'coach' gets fired for a losing-streak incompetence. Winning streaks are so much nicer! 4. ARCH EFFORT SPREAD: the total architecture effort can be distributed throughout the project, not as a big-bang up front. 5. FEEDBACK: by delivering increments in small and limited packages, we can get several kinds of feedback (value, cost, human reactions) which if negative, gives us a fair chance, to adjust our architecture, or maybe to adjust our false expectations 6

illustrations.ocrText: 4.3 Decomposition: part of Success Why is this Evo/Cleanroom method so good? A common sense explanation I would like to explain, in a focussed way, why this 'continuous agile architecture method' (aka Evo, Cleanroom) is so guaranteed to lead to success, or at least avoid failure. 1. We decompose implementation into small '2%' delivery increments. The biggest failure we can have, is 2%. When I gamble in Las Vegas, I bet $10 on Red. Walk away no matter whether I win or lose. Got it? 2. We measure the value results (not the 'code or stories' delivered) and the costs, at each step. Not at the 'end', at each step. 3. The architect is in the loop, and has the power to correct the architecture, to ensure value and costs. All real values-and-costs power, is in the design! 4. We try out the improved architecture immediately, to make sure it works. 5. We do not persist, or scale up, with things that do not work! What was Einstein's definition of a fool? 6. We cumulate value success incrementally. We ratchet it in. 7. We need to keep our eyes on something like 14 critical top-level value-and-resource requirements simultaneously. Stakeholders: the dozens, or more, sources of requirements which the designers need to know about, and make sure their design fits them. Value Process Manager: a person or team responsible for getting a best possible value stream flowing from the other people involved. illustrations.ocrText: 10.1.0 Defining a Scale of measure, Intro The core of this book, and the core of my Planning Language (Planguage, [B1]) is this subject. The 'Scale of Measure', or 'The Quantification Scale'. For short: 'Scale', with 'capital S' (indicating a 'defined concept'), which is a formal Planguage 'defined concept' (NOT 'term') in Planguage [P4]. All Planguage concepts can have synonyms, and all have a unique numeric tag synonym, the asterisk-number (*nnn). In Scale's case *132. Scale of Measure          Concept *132          [P4] A scale of measure defines a single scalar attribute dimension. It helps us 'quantify'. It is the basis for quantifying variable attributes. All scalar numeric level estimates, specifications, or measurements, are used with an implied (nearby and previous), or explicit, reference to a defined scale of measure. A 'Scale:' parameter specification defines the units of measure, and includes any other useful context, including Scale Qualifiers ('for defined [Tasks]'), normalizers ('per week'), and environment specification ('for Expert Hackers'). To avoid inevitable confusion, the Scale is NOT any sort of measuring or testing process. It is NOT what we call a 'Meter'

illustrations.ocrText: 10.1.0 Defining a Scale of measure: Scale Components The Scale has a finite set of tools, which we can think of as the 'possible components' of the Scale. Let me present them and define them, and justify them, to some degree. Then later we will see them in use, and in context. A full appreciation will take some more learning, but let us start by announcing the Scale toolkit. 1. Planguage parameter English name: The 'Scale:' parameter name. This refers to the official definition (*132, Scale). It allows us to re-use that definition, and to lock in that concept, without everybody having their personal, implied, in their head only, definition. You could also use -|-|- (the keyed icon), or Skala: (norwegian for Scale), or *1310.2. They are all synonym 'pointers' to the same concept. Scale: ...... -|-|- : .... 2. Possible Name Tag: The 'Tag For The Scale': not always necessary, but a possibility to refer to the tag and reuse it, from outside the current specification object. Otherwise, inside the spec object, there is only one option, by default. Suggested Scale Not Official: Scale: ..... 3. Units: The Units of Measure. Like % or Seconds. Scale: Seconds to ..... <do something> 4. WWWWW:

illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.0 Deriving 'numbers' on the scale of measure Most of the Planguage defined points on a Scale, with a simple definition, and concept icons. Past: any useful reference point. A performance or resource level achieved, in say, your old product or a competitor's organization Record: best in some class, state of the art. Something to beat. A challenge for you. An extreme Past ? Trend: a future estimate based on the Past Goal: the practical level needed for satisfaction, happiness, joy and 100% full payment! + Stretch: a level that is valued, yet presents a challenge to attain ? Wish: a level valued by a stakeholder, but which might not be feasible. Project is not committed to it ! Fail: a level needed to avoid a system failure of some kind [ ] Survival: a level needed for system survival Figure 10.2.0.2 Source CE [B1]. 'Fail' is just to the 'left' of 'Tolerable', but Tolerable is 'positive' (not Fail) so Kai and I adopted it for everyday use. Be positive. Survival is extreme (dead), and Fail is less extreme (think broken legs)

illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.3 Benchmarks.Trend The Trend level, was invented by Kai Gilb one day while we were flying in to Ericsson in Sweden. Planguage up to that point had no notion of a future benchmark. I failed to think of it for decades. Every tool we had (Past, Status, Record) for comparison with future plans, was past, and 'up to today'. It turned out that our client, Ericsson, liked it immediately, and used it, and that is a good sign of usefulness of a speculative idea. We were looking in the rear-view mirror before that moment, he who does not learn from history..., but in a fast-changing world, dealing with the future changes is more likely to be interesting than dealing with the 'ghosts of the past'. Ask marketing people. Ask military people. Ask politicians. You can specify as many Trend statements as you find useful. Your marketing people have this as their job. Strategic planners know they have to deal with the future, and they know the future is 'difficult to predict'. But that is no reason for not taking a stab at a Trend number. If it is crazy, hopefully someone will feel tempted to correct your gross misunderstanding. Example: Trend 2030 People = Babies, Problem = Malnutrition, Effec

illustrations.caption: A page from section 10.2.4 explaining why 'Ideal' is rarely used as a benchmark level in quality metrics. The page includes a photograph of an ICL Group Quality booklet titled 'Introduction to Quality Metrics, Issue 2'. The text describes a conversation with a Quality Director about setting realistic availability targets (99.8%) versus impossible ideals (100%), emphasizing that perfect quality req
illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.4 Benchmarks.Ideal We rarely use this 'Ideal' statement, because it is never past, future, or 'required'. 'Ideal' is an idealistic impossible dream, like '100% system availability forever'. The Quality Director of a large corporation and I were setting Corporate level product quality standards, in his office one day. He said, "well of course 'Availability' has to be 100%". Implied: 'we cannot be seen to aim for shipping sub-standard product or designing them intentionally, with a Goal like 99%'. In other words, 1% imperfection'. I reminded him that 100% of that quality would take infinite money and time, which we did not have at the moment. More practically I asked him to tell me what levels of that quality they were in fact shipping (the answer was something like 80%, which was normal for those products then). So we settled on a high impressive improvement as Corporate Standard like at least 99.8%. The job is not 'to be perfect', but to meet market needs, and to beat the competition (that's where the Record level comes in!). But I use 'Ideal' as a device when people try to specify unrealistic levels. I tell them, 'that would A Corporate Booklet with advice for quality metrics

illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.5 Benchmarks.Record The 'Record' benchmark performance level, is a useful benchmark, for the same reason all performance records are useful. 1. We know what is possible. 2. We know what has been impossible to now. 3. We know something about the conditions and technology to make it possible (we can replicate). 4. We know that our specified Goals, near or above this Record, might at best be very high risk. 'Record' is a risk management tool. 5. We know what we might have to have as a Goal to beat the Record, if we want to be competitive, survive, or have pride.. 6. Before you simply set a Goal to 'beat the record in 5 years time', you might like to do a Trend analysis, about where the best competitors will in fact be in 5 years time, and plan to beat that! Organizations that are in fierce international competition, need to use this background specification, together with their objectives, to formally remind themselves of what the plot really is. You cannot simply use management fuzz like 'We aim to be the best'. You need to translate into something like; 'We are going to beat the Trend of the Record by at least 20% at all times' (see the written plan!). Example: Record, 2020, Sp

illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.11 Constraints.Budget One Type of attribute is 'Resources'. Resources which we are going to plan for, are 'any limited supply' of 'fuel' or 'energy' which we need to have, in order to create, maintain and dismember a system. This includes the obvious, like money (different types), time, space, and qualified people. These are in limited supply, either because they are allocated as a Budget, or because there are some absolute limits, or because it would not pay off to allocate more, even if you could. The limit, or constraint, is generally called the 'Budget'. We can have a Budget for any time period, and any combination of [Scale Parameter] Conditions of interest. The Budget spec, corresponds to the 'Goal' concept used for stakeholder Values. But it is natural to use the conventional, and well-understood term 'Budget'. Example: Budget €5 million, For 2021, Area = Outsourced Software, Contract = Fixed Price. illustrations.ocrText: 10.2.12 Targets. Landing Zone (Intel) A 'Landing Zone' is simply an area on the Scale, rather than a point. You can also say it is a numeric area defined by 2 points on the Scale. This concept has best been taught and exploited by Intel (Erik Simmons). [R.LandingZones] "The LZ is a very powerful concept - I've rarely seen a tool adopted so fast in such a large organization." (Simmons , May 16 2003 Email) The Landing Zone (LZ) is a degree of freedom, given to a design team, to allow them to avoid maximizing any one attribute, at the expense of total optimization of the complete system. The designers can feel comfortable, and empowered, to make their own decisions; as long as they are in the LZ, even though they are at the bad end of it. They do not have to feel they must maximize this one attribute towards Goal and Stretch levels. The team's obligation is to the 'higher level' of critical performance on the market. They are making 'engineering tradeoffs' to benefit the higher good. The Landing Zone is a specific instance of a 'Range', a defined area between any 2 points on a Scale. illustrations.ocrText: Validating that the design will deliver enough value. ARE WE FOCUSED ON A CRITICAL GOAL AND DEADLINE? The Value Requirement levels specified (example, Goal 2030, 95%) is the driving force of the design process. ALL CONCURRENT DESIGNS MUST MEET ALL CRITICAL VALUE REQUIREMENTS: We look at those value requirement specs, and each one of our design problems is 'defined' by the total set of several value requirement statements. WE NEED TO RESPECT A SET OF OTHER CONSTRAINTS TOO: We need to ask ourselves, for example which design will get me to 95% by the year 2030 (including the other [conditions] detail, included in our problem specification)? WHAT IF WE HAVE NO VALID DESIGN IDEAS? If we have no design ideas at all, and neither does anyone else we communicate with; then we might possibly have a problem spec, for which there is no 'known' design solution. That means we cannot satisfy the requirement level, yet. WE NEED AN ENGINEERING DISCIPLINE TO VALIDATE MANY DESIGNS AND REQUIREMENTS: If we have several valid ideas, then the design process needs to get more-disciplined. The 'Provide Foods' strategy further decomposes int
illustrations.ocrText: Concrete Architecture, and Abstract 'Means Objective' Architecture. Some strategies are very specific things to do (Concrete). Other strategies (sub-architectures) are 'Abstract' meaning, we have not yet designed the concrete things to achieve them. We have just said 'how good those strategies have to be'; Or we have left the decomposition to a later specification, into more concrete detail. Improve World Health by 20% Abstract Objective Provide Pharmas Concrete Strategy Provide Foods Concrete Strategy Increase Patient Knowledge by 30% Abstract Strategy Provide Veggie Proteins Concrete Strategy Decrease Vitamin Content Costs by 50% Abstract Strategy Figure 3 G. Strategies can be concrete (just do it) or abstract (let us achieve it), but the abstract ones, need, at some point, to have concrete ideas behind them. Figure 11 K. Source [VP] Ch. 3. This is an insight into the nature of design, that I have observed. I do not recall any other source mentioning it. It is useful in understanding the design process, design responsibilities, and methods of leaving design open-ended (by initially using an abstract strategy).

It is time for more design, or more-effective design. Architecture Feedback! This numeric rigor is necessary (but practiced rarely) to avoid architects throwing in poor ideas, and quickly moving on to the next 'bad architecture work' they are going to do. As you will see in Chapter 12 (IET) they cannot simply throw in a high number, and move on. They have to document the evidence, their source, and 'themselves as estimator'. May I coin a term? illustrations.ocrText: 12.3.0.1 Estimating Future Levels of Value Quantities And now, my second favorite subject (after value quantification), possibly my 'best invention'. The Impact Estimation Table (IET). Kai Gilb likes to call it a Value Decision Table (VDT). It is. But I am sticking with the older name. It does not matter what you call it. It matters what it is. What is an IET? It is a model of the relationships between two levels of planning, let us call them Ends and Means (Means to the Ends). IET is an attempt to force us to think more deeply about what we really know and understand, about our objectives, resources, and strategies (aka designs, solutions, architecture, means). It is a tool like a Swiss Army Knife, with many purposes and applications. A tool for your professional life. It is similar to other table tools like Quality Function Deployment [P11], and Balanced Scorecard [S10]. But is significantly better, in terms of accurate modeling. The basic idea is simple: estimate the Impact of a Design on a requirement. Simple, but we do not cheat, like QFD and BSC. We do not estimate '+++' for an undefined quality (like 'Better Security') and a badly defined design like 'Modularization'. We try

illustrations.ocrText: 12.3.1.5 Estimating Future Levels of Value Quantities. Source of Evidence. The Impact Cell Window Evidence, as specified, can be wrong, misleading, incomplete, false: deliberately or inadvertently. The Rule [B1, IET Chapter, R8] that you must support your estimate, and your evidence, with an explicit traceable source, is a good, and old idea. This makes it possible to check things out independently of the 'evidence author': to review, to audit, to quality control, to interrogate. But do not underestimate the motivational effect it has when you 'demand' to know the source. People will quickly look for better sources, and better evidence. We will often, then, not have to check the source,; we can be sure enough, that people will 'do their best'. And that will be 'sufficient for purpose', or not. Do you want my evidence for this? Of course this presumes that the identity of the estimator, the Evidence provider, and the Source specifier, are logged and easily known. That creates responsibility, and motivation. Some of the prejudices against written bureaucratic cultures (and quite right these negative reactions were) were based on the 1920s pre-internet experiences. 'Written' is not now, what it was then. illustrations.ocrText: 13.3 Prioritization using background specs In my 'Evolutionary Value Delivery' culture, all Value requirements are not equal. We are going to start a stream of value-improvement deliveries. So we have to figure out which Value deliveries are smartest to deliver, early. There is no simple method to help us decide what to do first or next, which will be realistic, and to give the most satisfactory results. There are far too many different dynamically-changing factors, which influence a prioritization decision. So, our best suggested approach today is to collect prioritization-information, directly in the requirement specification. This background information can be used to help you decide which Value levels to prioritize. illustrations.ocrText: 1.0 Overview  One μStep at a time I have, for decades, developed a Planning Language, called 'Planguage'. It covers systems engineering planning, and it can handle very large and complex plans, which organizations and governments always have many of. But, it also can 'scale down', and handle very small, and simple, everyday problems, like setting your personal goals for an educational path, or planning family vacations together [3]. I've used it for simple family and personal matters, and it has been applied in large corporations [2] and governments, my clients and followers. This book is going to present 'Planguage' from a different angle. I will make no assumption about whether you have large or small projects, or both. Nor will I assume you want to master 'Planguage', ever. I will assume that you are interested in learning 'some tricks' or 'good ideas for planning'. That you, like me, need to pickup any 'language' by learning a series of simple practical ideas. Ideas of your choice, for your needs now. illustrations.ocrText: µAct Cross Referencing 2.1 Referencing. Plans can quickly get large, complex and changing. Even for relatively small projects. It amazes me how often I see plans and presentations with absolutely no attempt to systematically cross reference anything in other pages. The dead give-away, is a series of bullet points. They have no specific identity, not even a number. And you cannot reference them as '3rd bullet point in first paragraph'. A slight change, and you are referring to the wrong thing. Or worse, just a series of statements, sentences, with not even bullet points. So, some most-basic mechanisms you can adopt, for writing plans, is Tagging: applying Name Tags to things Referencing: Clear references to those Tags. illustrations.ocrText: µAct: Tagging 2.1.1 Tags Tags are not the 'real thing itself', not the 'bird'. They are merely a device for pointing to the thing itself. A thing, for example any planning specification, like a requirement or a design, can usefully have any number of name tags, or other pointers to it, like a symbol, icon or number. Nicknames, acronyms, and synonyms are useful. Once you name something, and name it uniquely, you can use that 'pointer' to find, or refer to, the thing itself. Quickly, and perhaps automatically, as with a URL like 'gilb.com'. One useful property of a Tag is that the thing it points to, like a requirement specification, can be updated, extended, corrected and changed. But the Tag allows us to be certain that it is the thing we intend to reference, in spite of changes. In Planguage we have some useful rules about Tags. 1. All Tags are written with Capital Letters, in each word of the Term. They can also be live digital links. 2. Tags can be 'made unique' in a large complex specification, by use of hierarchical tags. illustrations.ocrText: µAct: Synonymms. Don't argue about the meaning of terms 2.1.4 Synonymms When I use a word, Humpty Dumpty said in a rather scornful tone, it means just what I choose it to mean - neither more nor less. People, and especially my academic friends, seem to love to argue about the precise meaning of a term. I gave up that futile pursuit decades ago. Even if some people reach perfect agreement, it won't be long before someone decides to disagree. Humpty Dumpty decided to get control over the word 'Glory'. The solution is this: 1. Define a concept thoroughly, and improve the definition when possible and needed. Give it a 'version' or date. 2. Assign a Tag, or other device, for pointing to your definition. Allow any useful quantity of synonym 'pointers' to your definition. They should only point to one defined concept in practice. 3. Be clear to other people that 'this is our local definition of a concept. It is the best we have for now. We are not asking you to agree with anything in it. illustrations.ocrText: µAct: Icons 2.1.6 Icons Planguage uses Icons in planning, for a variety of purposes. They are short, visual, and multilingual. illustrations.ocrText: µAct Ambition Level 3.2 Ambition Level Cite the headline, or the management vision statement as a Vision, or User Story spec. Then, based on that, clarify and detail it, so that it is really operational in practice. The Ambition Level statement is perhaps the simplest and most common form of a requirement statement. Often a series of bullet points on a slide. A User Story is essentially the same thing. But many organizations allow it to be the only, and the last, statement of that requirement. Good enough for small and non-critical systems. But a probable disaster scenario, for larger and more critical systems. If not clarified, the 'government' or 'corporate' project can spend years, and millions, continuously failing, since nobody will know, or really be able to agree on, what the 'correct requirement' is. One option is to eliminate such statements from the specifications completely, and replace them with a clear and correct requirement. But I have developed a Planguage µAct where I politely, and diplomatically, thank the wise people for their vision, and then proceed to help them get what they really want, by translating the Ambition into clear, measurable, correct requirements.

illustrations.ocrText: µAct Scale 3:3 Scale Define a Scale of measure. This allows you to 'quantify'; to refer to levels of performance or values or qualities, on that Scale. And later define 'Meters' which are tests or measuring processes on that Scale (Speedometers). Scale is the most powerful µAct I can suggest. It makes you think, and discuss, very deeply about what you are trying to manage or design. It moves you from the world of craft and poetry to a world of engineering and maybe science. It is a key to successfully competing world-class. It is a key to managing complexity, and very large systems. It is a key to serious systems architecture [11, SEA]. It is a definition of the Value. We define a Scale once, for a requirement, and then we re-use it many times. A clear and useful Scale, for large systems, is rarely simple, un-like 'KpH', 'Volts'. It is highly tailored to your stakeholders, and to your environment. You can start with a scale pattern as in Competitive Engineering Chapter 5 [2]. But you will normally want to tailor it to your real, large, complex, environment, which cannot easily be generalized by outsiders. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Meter 3.5 Meter A Meter specification refers to a specific Scale. You cannot really specify a Meter for an undefined Scale. So the Scale is a prerequisite μAct. You need Scales to reason and think about requirements and their designs. You do not immediately need a Meter, until you want to actually measure your incremental value stream. And even then you can do without a Meter if the stakeholders are jumping for joy at every increment. You can use human stakeholder reactions as feedback to change. One advantage to defining, and in fact then 'designing' a Meter is that we can see its costs and qualities better. And perhaps get agreement on them, and fit them into resource constraints (deadlines, financial budgets). Meters have many qualities [9] and many cost dimensions. They can be very expensive. So sometimes they need to be 'engineered'. Designed to give the qualities you need at costs within constraints. Meters are a part of test planning for development and for operations. The μAct is to add this parameter to your specification vocabulary. A Meter specifies a way to measure activity on a defined Scale. Meters can be costly. And must be good enough for purpose quality. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Targets 3.8 Targets Defining Success Quantitatively: no doubt about commitments Targets are a set of future performance level types, primarily Wish, Goal, and Stretch. They are defined as Stakeholder aspiration levels (Wish), Project Commitment levels (Goal) and third priority use of residual resources - for marginal stakeholder Value (Stretch). These are more sophisticated options for planning than a simple 'requirement level'. The 'Wish' gives stakeholders the right to define their values, but the Goal give system improvers the right to balance multiple conflicting requirements from many stakeholders, as well as the right to balance the total load on limited resources. The 'Stretch' level gives increased competitive advantage when resources are available after all Goal commitments are delivered. I have also asked my BCS student planners to make sure each Sub-strategy had the following characteristics (a Decomposition rule for increments of value delivery) 1. Each sub-idea was tagged (D1 etc.), 2. Each sub-idea would arguably deliver some planned stakeholder value if delivered on its own, and 3. illustrations.ocrText: Examples of Design Constraints μAct Design Constraints 4.3 Design Constraints The restrictions on design selection. A Design Constraint is a direct stakeholder specification regarding the design itself. Part of good practice here is to document the circumstances. The responsible stakeholder, the motivation, the expectations, and a note of any circumstances which might cause them to back down. Design Constraints are a strange mixture; they are at once a design, and a requirement. Planguage has other planning μActs which restrict or encourage design indirectly such as 'Tolerable levels of Values', and 'resource constraints'. But a Design Constraint says 'you must use this design', or - 'you may not use another design'. Your actual designs are thus chosen for you in advance of your own design process. Or, designs you might have chosen are eliminated as possibilities. Design Constraints are not 'absolute'. They are like all other requirement ideas emanating from various stakeholders. They might be in severe conflict with the wishes of other, perhaps more influential, stakeholders. They may be unnecessarily severe with consequences for values and costs, and may need to be relaxed. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Value Strategies 4.4 Value Strategies There is a type of design/strategy which is not the normal 'design' 'thing to do' - in order to achieve higher objectives. It is a means to those objectives, but it is itself specified as a second-level objective. For example a 'better Office Environment' which we believe will lead to improvement in 'Employee Productivity'. Again, as with the Design Constraint (4.3) this is both a design (a means to achieve a higher objective) and a requirement (we have to achieve the value level, by some other means; to be determined). Since it is formulated as a Value, that means it needs to be specified with a Scale of Measure, and Scalar Constraints (like 'Tolerable') and a Target (like 'Wish'). The main point of this μAct is that we acknowledge that this is a 'Means Objective' [RalphKeeney.com] and it is not our primary Strategic Objective. That means that if the level of the Value Strategy, does not really deliver the expected higher-level objective, then, like any other proposed 'means' it needs to be replaced with a better means/strategy/value idea. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Impact Estimation 5.1 Impact Exactly how effective is your design for reaching our Goal on time? This is the breakthrough μAct in design. This μAct asks for a number, not 'confident words, based on hope', like 'very powerful'. The whole point of design, or strategy planning, or systems architecture - the 'means' to the 'ends' - is to find a set of 'means' which together, will help us cross the Goal (level) line, on time. We can, of course, do this without estimation, and without early incremental measurement of effectiveness. Just keep on trying out vague nice-sounding misinterpretations of your design idea, until you totally fail, are fired, defunded, and dishonored, no matter how many years it takes. Sound stupid to you? It is what people actually do. Observe and study history. It was Einstein's definition of insanity. Engineers, real engineers, not 'software engineers' (aka programmers, devs), nor 'sanitation engineers', have a series of early (key word, good economics) measurement stages, before committing design and scaling up use. illustrations.ocrText: µAct Costs' Impacts Sum 5.5 Costs' Impacts Sum The total design subtraction from finite resources is critically important to your project success or failure. It is getting to the required levels that counts, to avoid failure (Tolerable level) and to achieve Success (Goal, initially a Wish). So we have a μAct that allows us to compute (usually on a spreadsheet or app) this % effectiveness, where 0% means 'no effect' + or -. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Evidence 5.8 Evidence If you have no good evidence for your estimate, then why should we trust your opinion or judgement? It constantly amazes me that apparently educated intelligent people accept claims for designs and strategies [10] without even asking for the evidence. This would not be acceptable in law and science. But BS (Bad Specification) seems to be the norm in Software Engineering and Management. This is a dangerous act, on the part of the 'believer'. You will normally be severely disappointed. Will you ever learn? When did you last, write down evidence, for your assertions and estimates, in planning? Show me! So here is μAct Evidence, which says that 'for every design-effect assertion, there must be Evidence to back it up. It is incredibly widespread that individuals have not actually agreed to a clear definition of what a function is. They use the word to refer to all kinds of 'things' floating around in their consciousness. The worst common offense is calling 'designs' functions. There are of course multiple 'function' meanings in a dictionary. But in the Planguage Concept Glossary [6], there is only one. What a system does. In particular it is NOT, how well it does it (a quality). It is not how it does it so well (a design). It is not the resources needed to do it (a cost). Functions have in themselves no attributes, including no costs. A simple thought experiment proves this. Imagine a function with 0.0% Availability. How much does it cost? Zero. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Attack Detection 8.3 Attack Detection We should try to detect attacks of all kinds. As automatically as possible, as early as possible, before they get a chance to proliferate, before they can do significant damage. Attacks will happen, with unpleasant consequences. Some heroes will defend and defeat the attackers. But it would be better, and probably more cost-effective, if we had invested in systems (human and automatic) to detect attacks, as quickly as possible, at as low a cost as possible. This would reduce the consequential costs of dealing with attacks. This requires a mature willingness to invest in attack detection strategies. The alternative is to let the attacks happen, and clean up the mess. We see a lot of this in the news daily. And probably, in the systems with effective attack detections, we do not hear about them! I am not just speaking about the well-known security attacks. 'All kinds' includes competitors, government bureaucracy, ignorant and careless users, your own badly-architected and badly-engineered systems, top management's poor policy and priorities. The list is longer. μAct Implementation: Policy from Management: to Architecture and Project Manageme

The Plicons are defined in the Planguage Glossary [6] both in Drawn and Keyed (9.5.2) representations. The Drawn and Keyed Plicons are designed to resemble each other, as far as possible. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Iconic Languages.Keyed Plicons 9.5.2 Iconic Languages Keyed Plicons Refer to the Drawn Plicons basic ideas in (9.5.1). Keyed Plicons are constrained to those character combinations which are available, on most keyboards. Of course special soft-keyboard sets can be designed, and we can automatically convert a character sequence into a keyed icon. But we need to mainly simply key a keyed Plicon in on-the-fly. The original inspiration for these Icons was Bliss-Symbolics [19] but that was a universal language, and Plicons are a very small systems-engineering subset. One important characteristic of Plicons is that they are human-language independent. Another is that they pictorially are designed to resemble, in some way, the concept they represent. Another attribute is that they are usually very short (Fig. 9.5.2), compared to their Word Tags. Keyed Icons in particular are designed to combine with a stream of text. In my dreams, I have privately experimented with defining Planguage itself using the Keyed Icons as far as possible.[19]. But that is an academic exercise. A Logic Language. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Process Visualization 9.6 Process Visualization Visualizing Repeated Work Patterns Work processes are often visualized as repetitive loops. The concept of having an Entry and Exit Process for all main processes (Figure G15) is used in depth, everywhere in Planguage, and detailed patterns are in the Competitive Engineering book [2]. The basic ETX (Entry Task Exit = Process) idea (from production processes and via IBM published practices) is that we are too quick to start a work process, when in fact, the conditions that can allow it to succeed, are not present. A process of checking that the Entry Conditions are OK, might take a few minutes, and save you a few hours of wasted work, in your work process. The Exit process, before you release your work from the main process, is similar. You check that the conditions for release are met. Typically we use a Specification Quality Control [2] process, to check for defect levels in relation to Specification Standards (Rules [2]). illustrations.ocrText: μAct SQC Simple Data Collection Form 10.2.1 Spec Defect Measurement using SQC Simple Measurement by Sampling [21, 22] is better than old style Software Inspection [25] for several reasons. From 1987-2003 I learned, and practiced The IBM Radice/Fagan/Mills Inspection Method. In 1993 we wrote a book about our case study experiences, and our 400 process improvements over the IBM method. In 2003 CitiGroup, London asked us (Kai Gilb and I) to invent a radical simplification of Inspection, which we did and it worked well. Looking back we had experimented with elements of it much earlier. But it all came together in 2003. This is the SQC used by Intel (10.1). The revolutionary methods shift was: 1. We focus on measurement to prevent bad specs from moving downstream. 2. We do the measurement by random sampling. 3. We do not focus on finding and fixing spec defects; we focus on motivating development teams to learn to practice to standard early, so they can QC at early stages, and correct their practice for the rest of the project. illustrations.ocrText: µAct Defect Estimation 10.2.1.Defect Estimation Compute total defects one a page, and on all pages by inference and experience. This gives good enough accuracy to Exit or Not. This is essentially the formula for estimating the total defect density per page, based on a quick random sample, done by very few checkers (like 2). You can use this information to program a spreadsheet to do the maths for you quickly. This is based on long-term case studies and experience [2] that tell us that an individual finds about 1/6 of the spec defects that are actually on the page. A Team together finds about 1/3 of the defects. And 2/3 are not found by a team in a quick process. But they will surface in downstream testing (at 10x to 100x the cost of dealing with them now.) The simple fact that the whole sampling QC process is a same day, about 1 hour or so, process, means in practice, that you can do it early, and you can do it every so often in a long process. illustrations.ocrText: µAct Process Rules 10.3 Process Rules Process Rules are some specific inputs to a process, which define exactly what the process will do in detail. Rules as process drivers. I intend to look at Rules in the Standards section (18.). But I want to look at them from the point of view of a 'Process driver'. A Specification process, like 'Design Specification' for every draft spec it writes, the Author (the Designer who writes specs) needs, in principle, to check the specification, or relevant parts of it, and make sure it is in agreement with every Relevant Rule. In a later phase, self-checking (Fig. 10.2.3), the same is true. Read the Spec and check that every Rule is followed. Later, 'Buddy Checking' is obliged to follow the same procedure. Make sure each spec object (a 'design') complies with the same rules. During a Spec QC process, we are even more rigorous. On the spec sample, we are hoping to detect any potential deviation from the formal Design Specification Rules. But my personal experience, and the IBM [29] and Raytheon Experience [30] document that it delivers great measurable improvements to productivity and quality in a software organization. DPP is a Meta-Meta-Process (https://www.brsolutions.com/tag/meta-meta-process/): it helps all other processes get better. For example the concept definitions, like 'Function', the specification processes like 'Quantify a Quality', the Patterns for frequent Scales of measure like for 'Maintainability'. Things like that are ready to use, and also to modify in necessary directions (like defining [Scale Qualifiers]. (µAct 3.4) and their Conditions. The detail of possible tailoring is pervasive. The main idea to pick up here is that extensive tailoring-capability is built in, and at the same time extensive definition of things you can re-use is also built in. Re-inventing wheels is not necessary. Planguage captures a lot of development and planning experience, and it allows an organization to capture local domain-knowledge to supplement the core Planguage knowledge.
