illustrations.ocrText: μAct Concept Definitions 11.1 Concept Definitions The concept definition itself is the useful reality. The pointers to the concept are just tools, and they are not worth having arguments about (2.1.4 Synonyms). I noticed that people love to have arguments about the correct meaning of a word or term. Like 'agile', or 'lean', or (this evening, 'Patterns'. It gets worse: people can be so intent on arguing for 'their' correct definition of a term, that they do not put enough energy in a really deep and useful definition of the 'concept'. I have taken the trouble to define over 700 basic systems engineering concepts, as a basis for Planguage [6]. The definitions have remained 99.9% stable for decades. I think that is a healthy sign. I do not get attacked for the definitions. I hope that is a good sign, but maybe nobody cares much. It does not matter which terms, or other types of concept pointers, we choose to use; the important idea is to arrive at a single concept (to be unambiguous). And then hope it is brilliant, deep and clear. A Concept Glossary is quite different from a 'dictionary' which goes from a term, to multiple definitions. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Defined/Non-Defined distinction 11.2 Defined/Non-Defined distinction Make it clear when there is a definition available, and when you have to 'guess' The Planguage ideal is that 'all specifications are understood sufficiently well for their purpose'. So not everybody has to always understand every specification perfectly. But another related ideal is that 'Planguage specifications should be impossible to misunderstand, if that misunderstanding can lead to negative consequences'. It is an ideal. Planguage has a lot of μActs that help move us in that direction. So it is up to you to adopt the set of μActs that raise your organization's specification 'clarity' to the levels that pay off for you. We know that very slight misunderstandings, buried in a mountain of specification detail, can damage or kill, a whole project. Pervasive misunderstandings, many-per-page in a pile of documents, are certainly going to cause a series of subtle expensive problems, by project end. In general, the various tactics needed to have well-defined specifications, are a simple teachable 'clear technical writing' discipline. The low costs involved, are a small insurance price, to improve project succes

Any number of synonyms, national languages, abbreviations, symbols and numbers. There is a condition, of course, that in the context, that the pointer reference is used, it is unique. It does not point to more than one Glossary concept, or one specification object or specification parameter. We do not have to argue about the 'right word' or the 'right spelling in UK'. We can ignore pointers used by others, in favor of ones we find more useful. The Concept-pointed-to can change, be improved and updated. But the pointers will find their way to the update. We obviously need some sort of Version Control. This is usually done by date and time stamps, declaring the latest version the Master Version. In an app like ValPlan versioning (and undoing) is built in, and carefully controlled. In digital systems the pointers are URLs, URIs, or other local linking mechanisms. 'Method A is the most powerful for productivity'. Such statements are immature, useless, and dangerous (unless they are backed up by far more evidence). Planguage offers a basic way of clearly expressing such ideas, and in addition some useful special variations. illustrations.ocrText: µAct App Glossaries 11.11 App Glossaries Capture and Reuse Definitions Digitally It is not smart to fail to define critical terms: or to assume everybody else knows the correct definition, or to assume definitions are static, or to have 'too brief' definitions. But people fail in these respects pervasively. There is a reason for this bad practice. It takes effort to create a first class definition. A good definition might be quite long (not something you would drop in a parenthesis every time you used a term). And most of all, because such clarity and discipline is not unconditionally demanded by your organization (bad management). One easy solution to this, is to make use of digital tools, that can capture good definitions, and make them accessible as a hot link. There are quite a few of them, including Word, Powerpoint and https://protege.stanford.edu/ (Free), GraphMetrix.com (I'm investor) [41], and ValPlan (based on my CE [2]). ValPlan is especially useful, because it does all the other Planguage Stuff too! It is an inft'grated planning tool: but it is capable of easy capture of definitions, and automatic re-use. How many specified relationships do you have, for your requirements? The more we can document, and keep alive in our Requirements Object, the more 'intelligence' we are storing about our system, and about that particular requirement. Why take the bother? In short if we know about the relations, early, then we have a better chance to taken them into consideration early, like at an architecture stage. During for example an architecture review. Of course most methods for requirements do not take the trouble, The problem is that the problems downstream, in building or operating the system, will crop up, whether you like it or not. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Critical Relationships 12.8 Critical Relationships We must be explicit about critical relationships, to avoid failure. I love the term 'critical'. It refers to the medical term, critical for life, critical to avoid death, critical to have success. One μAct is to make sure that all critical values, have a formally defined, and agreed, level like 'Tolerable' which makes the critical border clear, to designers and developers. The exact level itself, might not be a cliff drop, in practice, but it is important to define, agree - and work to keep well away from the 'intolerable' area. Constraint specification is a tool to prioritize planning and development around that dangerous level. Too many practices and methods focus on the success target ('Goal'), and forget to articulate the critical level. This can lead to sub-optimization; the use of resources to get to the success levels, may steal resources for survival with respect to other and critical values. Another example of watching a critical relationship is in stakeholder identification, and analysis [14]. illustrations.ocrText: μAct Rules to Specs Relations 12.09 Rules to Specs Relations[36] Even the simplest Rule of good practice, probably needs to be stated and enforced. Rules are the standards for specification, for writing ideas down. There is a strong relation between the Rules, and what then gets written down. There is a relationship between the specifications, and the rules that were applied. There is a strong relationship between Rules and the concept of specification defects, as found in Specification Quality Control [2]. Failure to follow a Rule is the very definition of a Specification Defect. It surprises me how many organizations have no Rules for specification whatsoever. They just leave everybody to write as best they can. But that is how we get a result of very ambiguous and unclear planning, and consequent project failures. That is like having no traffic rules, more accidents are bound to happen. We need freedom for good practices, but freedom to write bad technical specification is not in anyone's interest. illustrations.ocrText: μActs Levels of Concern 13.1 Stakeholder Levels [14] Stakeholder Hierarchical decomposition is a useful way to identify high-value subsets of general types of stakeholders. Stakeholders, for even medium-sized systems, can be a very large number: at least 'dozens'. But if you take the trouble to imagine and document sub-sets of the initial stakeholders you identify, you will usually find that there are very interesting sub-sets of the more-generic stakeholder. Try 'nurses' or 'teachers' for example. The advantage of taking the trouble to do this decomposition is that you are more-likely to identify special stakeholders, of high value, high criticality to your project, and high possibility of early incremental value-delivery to them. You are more likely to discover that these sub-stakeholders have special values, special value levels, and special value level deadlines. They will also consequently need special strategies or designs to satisfy those values. This is a 'decomposition' process, of course. illustrations.ocrText: μActs Levels of Concern 13.9 Levels of Risk Risk needs levels and relations to manage it. We all like the simple idea of making things simpler. But this book, you may've begun to realize is completely different. It does not merely say 'things should be simpler'. It defines simple and simplicity in a quantified structure, so that we can really simplify large-and-complicated systems. We can apply engineering principles to simplify things. This quantified structured definition is a necessary basic pre-requisite for really good communication about the simplification problem. This clear (= simple) communication, about simplification, is necessary, when many people, over long time, and distances, are going to work together, to make better large-scale system, like for corporations and government purposes. [G13 (Gov), G14 (SP)]. We always quantify all variable factors: objectives, values, qualities, resources, so that they are clearly defined and understood. Most planners use nice sound-bite words for value. 2. We deal with many critical objectives simultaneously, not just a few dominant ones. 3. We are willing to analyze a very wide set of critical stakeholders, not just 'customers' and 'users', to determine their myriad but critical values and constraints. 4. We will test, and measure, decisions on a small scale, and adjust them immediately when the results dictate (scientific experiment). 5. We will prioritize incremental delivery of decisions, based on reasonable and credible estimates, of all critical objectives and constraints. 6. Our primary focus is delivering a measurable profitable value stream, early and continuously, and decisions must support this primarily. 7. illustrations.ocrText: 1.2.2.1    Decision-eering Principles: why they make things simpler 1. IMPERFECT DECISIONS: All decisions can be improved, and should be continuously improved after initial drafts. You do not have to worry if your decisions are researched correctly, and are perfect. You can get on with the job of delivering value. 2. SCIENTIFIC METHOD: All decisions need to be treated as a hypothesis, until disproven. We let measured facts decide if we are right in our decisions (simple, and reliable), not meetings and arguments (complicated and untrustworthy). 3. LOGICAL BASIS: The factual basis for decisions needs to be documented, traceable, responsible, reviewable, quality controllable, and transparent. This simplifies quality control, like reviews and inspections, and root cause analysis. The evidence is captured, when things happen. Simpler to remember the decision basis. 4. DECISION AGILITY: Even initially-successful decisions need to be reversible or adjustable, as circumstances change. This simplifies the problem of being stuck with irreversible decisions 5. illustrations.ocrText: Would you like to 'never fail'? 2.8 Failure Avoidance Principles Create a high efficiency value stream, and stop quickly, when it does not pay off. Here are the basic failure avoidance principles. 1. KNOW EVIL: Define Failure conditions explicitly, and agree to avoid them. Like 'Tolerable-Value-Levels', and other constraints. 2. OUTSMART EVIL: Avoid Failure conditions; by conscious design, architecture and strategic planning. Use 'Design to Costs'. 3. CHOOSE GOOD: Prioritize low-risk partial-strategy increments in your value stream, to build high delivery-efficiency value-cumulation. 4. RESPOND FAST: Learn early, frequently rapidly, and measurably, what works, and what doesn't. Apply that knowledge immediately to 'accentuate the positive', and 'de-accentuate the negative'. 5. LIMIT LOSSES: Never bet your 'wad' (budget), never more than about 2% of it. Be prepared for a potential 'total loss' on a 2% step, but learn fast, and avoid too-many loss-steps. When it is obvious that the goals cannot be reached, don't adjust the goals, adjust the action steps. Confucius (551-479 BCE) I HEAR AND I FORGET. I SEE AND I REMEMBER. I DO AND I UNDERSTAND. -Confucius Page 42 of 158 © tom@Gilb.com.

illustrations.ocrText: Basic PENTA definitions. 'Penta' Definitions: The Agile Penta Conflict Balance The PENTA is a simplified model of 5 basic conflicting forces in any system, which can be adjusted to give a more optimum balance. The PENTA Forces are: Scope, Values, Efficiency, Resources, and Designs. 'SVERD' (Norwegian for "Sword"). 1. Scope: is the specified set of stakeholder- and system-functions (what it must do) and constraints (what it must not do). Scope draws a border around a given system. 2. Values: is the specified set of stakeholder values ('wants', 'needs', 'wishes', 'visions') and system qualities, including system performance attributes ('potential values' for stakeholders). 3. Efficiency: is 'effectiveness-to-costs ratio'. Effectiveness includes all stakeholder-values actually delivered. The costs are life-cycle costs, not just 'capital' costs. This is a view outside the black box of Designs. 1. Resources: are any critical and prioritized, set of limited resources for the system lifecycle, such as time, money, people, space. 4. Designs: are any types of 'implementable ideas' (designs, strategies, architecture, solutions) which we use, in order to deliver a 'best available' balanced de

The left side contains principles 1-5, the right side contains 6-9. A 3D rendered golden/bronze dodecahedron structure appears in the bottom right corner, labeled "A set of Penta portals". The principles discuss reality limits, tradeoffs, priorities, clarity, i
illustrations.ocrText: The Agile Penta Conflict Penta Principles: 1. Reality Limits: there are some real limits to what is actually possible in the real world for products, services and process efficiency; The Penta is a tool to model those limits, and to allow us to plan useful balanced realities. 2. Tradeoffs: in general, we can improve any system dimension (like cost, usability), up to a real-world limit, by reducing, modifying, or eliminating some other Value requirement, or Designs, anywhere in the Penta. 3. Priorities: If we decide to prioritize a Value performance level of any Penta requirement, we can potentially do so, by adjusting one or more other Penta requirements, and/or Designs, of lesser priority. 4. Clarity: The clearer, and more detailed, a Penta Requirement is, the more likely that we can logically decide on the necessary specifications, for other conflicting or co-operative requirements (Using Planguage [CE] logic, and specification). 5. Interconnectedness: we have to assume that any Penta requirement, if changed, can influence several other requirements, both negatively, positively, and in dynamically unpredictable ways. 6. Computability: to the degree we specify Values and Resources

illustrations.ocrText: Logical Relations There are some immutable relations between the Pents. 1. Values are a relationship between Stakeholders, and the Scope. 2. Designs are the necessary mechanism for delivering any Values. 3. Designs determine the necessary level of all Resources needed, of all types, at all times in the system lifecycle. 4. Efficiency can be viewed in many various, but useful, ways; but is always computed as some 'set of Values' over some 'set of Resources'. 5. Scope determines Resources needed, but only as a multiplier for a given Values-level set. If Values are negligible (like 0% availability) the resources needed for an 'infinite Scope system' is zero. 6. Efficiency is Values/Resources which is determined by Designs. 7. Designs cannot (should not) change Scope, but a conscious change in Scope (a 'Scope sacrifice') can enable different valid Designs; which enables better Values/Costs = Efficiency Scope Values Designs Efficiency Resources Caption Page 59 of 158 © Tom Gilb 2022 PENTA

illustrations.ocrText: Stakeholder Values are the main priority, and main cost-drivers The second fifth (quint) of the Penta, is 'Values', which is short for 'Stakeholder Values' and 'Product Values'. The nearest we get to 'Values' in Iron Triangles is 'Quality', which never has, in the literature [1, 2, 3] an acceptable definition, is not plural (Qualities), and is not defined measurably. In a typical average real project, we easily identify over 50 critical stakeholders [SE] (like the CTO, and EU Law), each one of which has at least one, usually more, 'Values' that they want, dealt with, in your project (or they will not buy it, use it, recommend it, or allow it to be legal). There is nothing simple, like 'The Quality'. It is more like 'over 200 Critical Stakeholder Values', define the measurable, and deadline-driven, deliverables of the project. Failure to deliver one single critical Value (like system availability for a telecoms service, or crash safety for a car, or usability for an app) is enough to doom your project to total failure. illustrations.ocrText: Multiple, long-term and short-term resources Resources play a number of different roles in project management. And everybody knows how to quantify resources, like time, money, space. Most people do not know how to quantify resources like reputation, brand image, confidence, credibility, sustainability, digital transformation, AI Ethics: but marketing people, and others, do. If a resource is infinite, the project does not have to worry about it. But few resources are really infinite, as we are experiencing planetarily. That is why we set budget limits on money, and time, and other resources, often too early in a project, before the 'Values that consume resources' are known, agreed, quantified, and designed for. The next stage, after 'budgeting too early', is estimation. The Iron Triangle literature [1, 2, 3] spends considerable space discussing various ways of estimating resources; most of which strike me as bad and obsolete. Then there is project resource consumption accounting. 'How much over budget' are we today? illustrations.ocrText: Designs: Design-to-Value and Design-To-Cost The 'Designs' is our simple word for any 'implementable ideas' we choose; to reach our ends (Values, Efficiency, Scope, Resources). 'Designs' has many synonyms, such as means, architecture, strategies, tactics, solutions, engineering specification. In addition it is too common, that Designs are incorrectly designated as 'functions', and 'objectives', by people who do not have a well-considered glossary [CE, Concept Glossary]. The danger there (of confusing Functions and Objectives, with Designs) is that they are taken as fixed requirements, instead of the more-agile 'Design' concept of opening up the design-process options, of a rich proliferation of emerging Design options (options which have better Values and Resources, than previous options) to solve the eternal problem of Product 'Efficiency': sufficient Values for lowest Resources costs [SEA]. To confuse us, one person's 'Designs' can be delegated to sub-supplier levels, and 'become' their 'requirements' ('we require you to build our design', and DO NOT 'improve' our design, however bad it is'). It consists of 12 pentagons. Da Vinci was duodecedronnic, too. The PENTA can be applied as a 'process cycle', where our focus moves from any quint to another, skipping as desired, to consider areas of interest. This is a systems engineering [CE] process (not merely a Project Management process). As Dr. W. Edwards Deming also orally confirmed my hypothesis, re PDSA [5], there is no designated start point. You can dive in anywhere, at any time, for any reason. This is more true, when the cycles are rapid (daily, weekly) rather than in some 'big bang Waterfall' process, with years for a cycle. Yes, this is a very advanced engineering view of process agility [AG, AE] compared to simpler popular 'agility' methods, which lack Value, Design; and most of the ideas in the PENTA. illustrations.ocrText: Innovation How does the Penta relate to Innovation? A very detailed answer is in the reference [IN] which includes the book, 'Innovative Creativity' [IC Book]. Here is a necessary definition from the book: Innovative: significant improvements in qualities, values and costs, compared to previously. • novus: 'new', Latin • but the main shift in thinking here is that, it is not the 'Designs' which are 'new' it is the 'Values for people', that are 'new' • In addition, to Innovative Stakeholder Values is the desire for reduction in the resources needed to develop and maintain those values, which is dealt with by Resources, and Efficiency (Values/Resources) • another term, more specific: is 'Value Innovation' • our main focus, is not 'innovation' generally, in itself ('new stuff') but it is 'Value(s) levels', that we would like to have, as 'new' in the future. So the Penta provides a framework for defining the real Innovation (New Stakeholder Values) while avoiding the illusion of innovation (simply looking for 'new technology' itself). illustrations.ocrText: Synergy: How does Penta manage it? Synergy is when 2+2 ≠ 4. Maybe 5, maybe 2.5. who knows. Synergy is when two or more forces interact to give a result that is not a simple additive effect. Normally we are interested in geometric effects where 2+2 > 4. But on occasion we have to suffer Negative Synergy (Tom also likes to call it 'Thrashing'): either because we are unaware of it, or because it allows us to reach an higher priority (a trade-off), or because we do not know how to eliminate it, without penalties (negative side-effects), yet. Penta offers several tools to manage synergy, which are essentially the same as risk management tools, because Negative Synergy is risk. Positive Synergy is Opportunity. 1. Incremental value delivery, with small increments, result and cost measurement expose synergistic effects early, so they can be avoided or exploited. (Evo method, [CE, Evo Chapter]) 2. Planguage [CE] and Modelling in gilb.com/ValPlan help us keep track of relations, between all the Penta Factors; with synergy potential. 3. illustrations.ocrText: MANAGING the balance of these critical factors is a method for successful compromises The Penta is an attempt to identify the key interrelating forces that interact with each other when solving a problem and how they relate to each other. The issues of scope, values, efficiency, design, and resources, provide us with how to think about different approaches to solving problems. These issues have four dimensions: 1. Initial constraints 2. Relationships between them 3. Side effects of these relationships 4. How they may change over time The purpose of the Penta is to provide guidance on solving problems with different constraints. The Iron Triangle was always a simplistic model ignoring the relationship between quality and speed. Lean demonstrated that if one focuses on removing delays speed goes up while quality goes up. They are not in conflict with each other. But to make this happen the concepts of the Penta must be considered. illustrations.ocrText: Agile simplification: the barriers to simple simplifications Many problems do not easily allow us to simplify a system (product or process) immediately. Because: 1. COMPLEXITY: There are too many intertwined factors influencing any judgement about 'if we have indeed simplified well enough'. 2. CHANGE:Many of those complexity factors are changing continuously, some dramatically. Todays simplification risks are becoming quickly obsolete. 3. DIFFERENT SIMPLICITY: In the long term, the best simplification might turn out to be a series of different simplifications, year by year, depending on how the influencing factors change. 4. SIMPLICITY OBSOLESCENCE : The value results of one 'simplification' might be reduced, when the influential factors change in the future. 5. CONCURRENT SIMPLICITY: We might actually be best served by a concurrent set of simplifications, for different sets of stakeholders (like countries and age groups). One simplification at one time, might be a bad compromise for many stakeholders. 6. SIMPLICITY ENVIRONMENTS: The technology, politics, social systems or economics, might inhibit (constrain us from using) some really good simplifications. 7. AGILITY: In conclusion

illustrations.ocrText: Conditions, principles, and tools for solving the problems of long-term simplification 1. FEEDBACK: simplicity is a design hypothesis. We hope and believe that a specific design, will be 'simple' in some dimensions. But, in a complex environment, it might fail, so we need feedback from the 'simple idea' implementation, to confirm or deny, that it really is simple. 2. REQUIREMENT RELEVANCE: the specified set of values and scope, for a set of critical stakeholders, needs to be a complete, and correct, set. If there is any fault in these points, even in one critical requirement, then the resulting 'simple' system might be irrelevant, to the real world. 3. EXPORTING SIMPLICITY: the moment the successful simple design, is exported to an environment with a different set of Values and Scope: the successful simple design risks becoming irrelevant, or 'less relevant'. 4. ENGINEERING CULTURE: there needs to be an engineering culture, to keep track of multiple requirements, and potential designs; to enable adjustment to the real world quickly. illustrations.ocrText: PRINCIPLES OF MULTI-DIMENSIONALITY SIMPLIFICATION 1. illustrations.ocrText: A Framework for Changing the Tech Ecosystem How Do We Tackle Complex Problems? "Today, technological harm is outpacing current solutions. We see the effects in seemingly disparate areas — fragile democracies, degraded mental health, growing political polarization, conspiracy theories going mainstream, and distrust of journalism and institutions. The issues we face are complex and they are ever-evolving. But they are not disparate, they are systemic. Where Do We Go From Here? Our natural human response to a challenge is to search for an actionable solution. Something that we can do, ideally now. But complex problems require systems-level solutions. Thus, we must elevate the discussion beyond harms and towards a systems perspective. Inspired by Donella Meadows' 12 Leverage Points to Intervene in a System, we developed a simplified framework of leverage points for how to intervene in the extractive tech ecosystem. The Leverage Points Framework shows that: • Change happens at multiple levels with different degrees of impact. Generally, leverage increases from left to right on the framework. illustrations.ocrText: What has shocked you the most about the British Empire? The leanness of its bureaucracy. The British Empire was all about gaining access to the resources, using the of minimum human resources. The British administration of India in 1930's of example, consisted of a mere 2,000 civil servants running a land mass which would include India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Today that British Civil service probably employs that many diversity and engagement officers. The East India Company began as a very lean organisation. Even when it had become the largest commercial force in the world, for the first 20 years of its life it operated out of the house of its governor, Sir Thomas Smythe. In many ways the East India Company was a model of corporate efficiency: 100 years into its history, it had only 35 permanent employees in its head office. Yet this 'skeleton crew' managed to control trade, through the military conquest, subjugation and plunder of vast tracts of southern Asia. illustrations.ocrText: The Historical Background of Inspection 3 at Western Electric Co., AT&T's manufacturing subsidiary in the 1920s. One of Bell Labs major software development organizations with 200 staff reported the following experiences with Inspection in 1986: • 14% productivity increase (for a single release); • better tracking and phasing; • early defect density data improved by ten times; • staff credit Inspection as an 'important influence on quality and productivity'. 1.1.3 Subsequent Improvement and Extension of Inspection Defect Prevention The Inspection technique was built on by Carole L. Jones and Robert Mays at IBM (Jones, 1985) who created a number of useful enhancements (see Figure 1.3): • the kickoff meeting, for training, goal setting, and setting a strategy for the current Inspection cycle; • the causal analysis meeting; • the action database; • the action team. IBM fulfilled Fagan's original intention of process improvement by turning Inspection from predominantly a defect correction process into also being an effective defect prevention process (Mays, 1990). A paradoxical problem with Inspection is that even a pale imitation of the 'real thing', such as a walkthrough, can be quite effective at improving software quality by finding some important defects. Even doing Inspections badly can give quite good results. This is particularly evident when no type of review at all has been performed to date. However, the 'good' really does work against the 'best' in this case, as the benefits from doing real Inspection properly would be far greater. The tragedy is that many people are satisfied with the 10% improvement, and never explore the potential for 100% or more improvement. illustrations.ocrText: 26 Software Inspection 2.3.3 Organizational and People Benefits The benefit of Inspection for most software professionals is that their work is of better quality and is more maintainable. Furthermore, they can expect to live under less intense deadline pressure. Their work should be better appreciated by management, and their company's products will gain a quantifiable competitive edge. It is important that the individual software professional be made fully aware of these benefits. Otherwise they may take the short-term view that Inspection is just an extra task which interferes with their already high-pressure schedule. Inspection also tends radically to improve the quality of the documentation standards and source documents, thus having a greater effect than a review or walkthrough on the total development activity across all areas of the organization (see Figure 2.2). Inspection has particular benefits for all professionals on the team. In picking up the culture of the organization, in being exposed to the best of other people's ideas, but also becoming aware of their own and others' weaknesses, professionals are given strong positive motivation to change for the better. It is even more important that the product when exited is of the quality which is required, so that the software development process which will take place next on this product will not waste developers' time. illustrations.ocrText: 116 Software Inspection 7.2 Process Control Concepts Process improvement is based on the fundamental concepts of 'process control', first developed by Shewhart and later by Juran and Deming. The nature of a process is dynamic. Events happen in a time sequence, and 'flow' through various stages. Some famous process control models are shown below. 7.2.1 Process Control Model: Shewhart Cycle The Shewhart Cycle is shown in Figure 7.3. It is composed of four steps which form a continuous cycle: 'Plan, Do, Check (or Study), Act'. Starting at the 'Plan' step to outline what will be done, the carrying out of the main task is the 'Do' step. The task is then checked (this is also called 'study'), and action is taken as a result, which results in further plans. Thus the basic process which is carried out (the 'Do') is being continuously improved through what is learned in checking the task, and in the actions taken as a result. This is continuous process improvement. Note that continuous process improvement has no stopping point, because if it did come to an end, it would not be a continuous process. The process improvement part of Inspection is based on this process cycle. 7.2.2 Process Cont

illustrations.ocrText: 148 Software Inspection Source Document Status: Exited from Inspection One of the basic principles of Inspection is that any source documents used have ideally already been checked themselves and have successfully 'exited' from Inspection earlier (see Figure 8.7). If they have not exited, we must proceed with great caution and explicit recognition of the untrustworthiness of our sources (marked on copied sources given to checkers) 'NOT EXITED'. Checking against an un-exited source can lead to a situation where defects in the source document are 'successfully' preserved in the product. What About Sources at the Very First Inspection? At initial start-up of Inspection, no source documents have previously been Inspected and exited successfully. We must be fully aware that such uncontrolled, un-exited documents could and often do contain between seven and seventy defects per page. A sound practice, indeed a generic entry requirement ('all sources must have exited'), is to Inspect and exit the source documents, or at least a sample of them, before continuing work creating and checking the task outputs. illustrations.ocrText: 8 The Inspection Leader 167 The primary role assignment rule: Maximize total major issues found by the team. The secondary role assignment rule: Assign roles with regard to the talents and interests of the individuals involved - and with their agreement. 8.8.2 Types of Roles There are three types of roles: document roles and checklist-defined roles and procedure-defined roles. Document Roles An individual checker is given a special responsibility to pay particular attention to one or more of the documents used in the checking process. This assignment is in addition to the candidate product, which every checker looks at very carefully. A document role contains two responsibilities: • check the document itself for issues; • exploit the document to discover issues in all other documents. A document role is assigned in the master plan to individual checkers. It is assigned using the document tag. It can be assigned for all checked document types (sources, products, checklists, rules, Inspection procedures). Hypothetical Example: Calculation of Inspection Costs and Savings Suppose that 100 defects are produced per week, which would cost 30 minutes each to find and fix at Inspection time. If we assume that Inspection is 80% effective (this is probably rather high for an immature Inspection process, 50% may be more conservative), then Inspection can find 80 of them, for a total cost of 40 hours. There will be 20 defects which will slip through the Inspection net and be looked for in test execution. We will assume that accumulative testing is also 80% effective at finding errors. The cost of finding and fixing an error in testing is at least ten times more than finding it before it has been built, so the cost to find and fix one of the errors is 300 minutes, that is, five hours, and 16 defects will be found. Why Inspect Documents? Documentation is used as a vehicle for written information about ideas, requirements or achievements in order that other people may use this information for various purposes. However, these documents are written by error-prone humans, and therefore contain defects and ambiguities. It is evident from studies of the relative cost of fault correction that it makes sense to stop these documentation defects occurring as early and as efficiently as possible in order to minimize product costs to ourselves as developers, producers, maintainers (see Figure 14.1) and users. It makes sense for any organization to reduce costs by reducing the incidence of defects being propagated from proposal through to end product/service use as early as possible in the product development life cycle. However, the Defect Prevention Process provided a more comprehensive process which could be readily taught and implemented by other development organizations. The process uses a simple concept - do causal analysis on your defects and implement changes that will prevent those defects from recurring. However, it is far from simple to implement methods and procedures that can be successfully deployed within a development organization and bring results. In this respect, the Defect Prevention Process is similar to Inspection, which also has a simple concept - have people look at the development work products to find defects - but is likewise far from simple in actual implementation. There are four key elements of the process which are integrated into the development process. Software development is usually divided into process steps (also called 'stages' within IBM), such as design steps, code, unit test, function test, and so on. The Defect Prevention Process is applied at each process step, including the test steps. The following description summarizes a typical application of the

illustrations.ocrText: Where is the power that determines success and failure? 3.0 Stakeholder Analysis Who are your critical stakeholders? [11] The focus of some methods, on users (User Story, UX) and customers is a failure path. There are too many powerful stakeholders who can kill your project or system, like legal bodies, like EU, think GDPR Laws. So you have no choice but to make a deeper analysis of critical stakeholders: defined as stakeholders that can determine success or failure. Some stakeholders will have values to improve, and deliver, which is their definition of success. The detailed discipline of stakeholder analysis is in my 2021 Stakeholder Engineering [11] book, a mere 163 pages, which explains why it is not all on this page. The basic process is simple. illustrations.ocrText: Partial Success, Value-Levels 3.3 Constraint Values Defining the worst acceptable case Many quantitative methods for requirements and objectives, just rely on the single concept of the 'goal level', or the 'target' [13, OKR]. I have found that defining a 'value constraint', a minimally acceptable level (or several such levels for different conditions), in addition to a target (a success level), is necessary, and useful. We have several defined concepts in Planguage to do this (Tolerable, Fail, Minimum (used at Intel), Limit). But for most purposes we use the 'Tolerable' concept. A 'Tolerable level' is defined as 'not intolerable'. 'Intolerable' is defined as a degree of failure. In terms of this Success discipline, which has a secondary objective to 'not fail', this is an important tool. Our first priority, in planning, design, testing, and operation is to, at least, achieve a minimum Tolerable level of performance. The Tolerable level clearly defines our first priority - survival. It might also be used in contracts, as a minimum level for any payment. From the 'edge point' of tolerable, we have a 'tolerable range', which stretches to the next defined 'success' point (Goal, Wish).

Some types of Value Objectives require foresight, responsibility, technical insight, and early investment. They are not for 'managers who just want a quick win', and who do not really care about the long range success of their system. For example, those who do not care about the lifetime annual operating costs, and the maintenance costs. If you scan the map of typical system qualities (Fig. 3.9) perhaps you can sort the qualities into two groups. Those that are of immediate interest from 'day one' of the system (like Throughput, or Availability); and others which might not be critically interesting, until later in the life cycle, like Portability and Extendibility. We could take the short-term success view of our system, product, service - by focussing on the success levels of the immediate operational short-term qualities. But, mature planners will want to take action on the long term qualities, to avoid later failure. This is what some organizations disguise as 'new updated systems', at great cost and dangers. Do not promise what you are not sure you can deliver! Success is not 'reaching someone's over-ambitious dream'. Success is reaching realistic, committed, value levels; when many conflicting interests and factors, are simultaneously considered. I would suggest a term here: Mature Success Management. Another weakness with conventional target-setting methods [13], in addition to the lack of a constraint level, like 'Tolerable', is that the specified target is, or seems to be, unquestioned. 'The customer is always right'. The trouble is that: 1. The stakeholder is in ignorance of what is technically and economically possible within deadlines, 2. The stakeholder, who dreams of a high level of performance, is not responsible for any nasty side-effects on other stakeholders, which their dream-level might cause. illustrations.ocrText: Success Levels 3.11 Levels of Value Objectives Some objectives are supporters, some are the real Stars. Some objectives support higher-levels of objectives. Reaching those 'supporting objectives' is a strategy in itself - for reaching the next level up, of objectives. There is often a hierarchy of success objectives, which we need to manage and understand. The logic of 'ultimate success', means that each level, must reach success levels, so that the top level (the ultimate point of it all) can be a success. If you are 'personally', or your team is, responsible for any level, then your Success is measured in terms of you reaching the planned levels of your objectives. That implies that you should have a lot of freedom to plan and adjust the supporting objectives, the levels below. They are actually your strategies (Strategic Objectives). Similarly, you do not have responsibility for the objectives, at levels above you. Somebody else does. You just have to do your part to reach your objectives set', and to hope that our 'planning theory', that if you do reach them, the higher level will be delivered. It should be explicit, and be given to people and groups who are motivated and capable of delivering results. Nothing simple like 'the project manager'. We gave one example of various forms of responsibility specification in Figure 3.10. Figure 3.12 is another example. My experience is that most plans, have no detailed specification of people and instances (papers, plans, organizational units). There is no traceability, and no responsibility. The tools to review plans, by tracing the origin and responsibility for details in the plans do not really exist, in a large organization; for example government health organizations [Govneering, 15]. This 'unknown responsibility' situation is inviting failure, and not helping us achieve real success. illustrations.ocrText: Systematic Success 4.1 What is a System? And Why is 'system' vital to success? A Primary reason for failure, and for lack of success, is that we fail to consider the whole real system we are dealing with. For example we are building an IT system, and focus primarily on the hardware and software, while forgetting - taking no explicit responsibility for - the dataware and peopleware [17,PoSEM] aspects of the system. Not to mention the qualities and costs! Related to this failing, is that we fail to identify, define, analyze, and design, for critical aspects of the system we are looking at. For example most 'system' definitions focus on the idea of 'interconnected parts' and stress 'Functions' [Figure 4.1 B]. Indeed a dominant system mapping tradition is in terms of connected parts or functions [Figure 4.1 C], but not in terms of values, qualities and resources, or designs. Or, we put words in a circle, but do not define what type of system attribute (function, quality, activity, state, cost) is there, nor do we define it well enough for purpose. illustrations.ocrText: Limiting your attention and priorities 4.2 System of Interest Everything is connected A 'system of interest' is a set of system elements where you are focusing your attention. Focus, prioritization, is necessary. But because of the subtle interconnectedness of remote and unknown factors there is a real possibility, almost a certain probability, that something outside of your defined system of interest, will either have a severe negative effect on your success results (like new laws affecting your services), or will be a big missed opportunity you do not even know about (like lost sales in an uncharted market). This is one reason I recommend thorough Stakeholder analysis [11, SE]. Another level of defence against bad happenings, from outside of your declared system of interest, is Feedback - of all kinds, measures of values and costs, but also social media and complaints. It will require a 'sensitive antenna', early, frequent feedback, rapid analysis, and rapid response to the situation. You cannot really consider 'everything', but you can prepare defenses against the results of the 'unexpected' - to improve your Success. Here is an intro to 'systems of interest' https://www.sebokwi

illustrations.ocrText: Project Science, Success Science 5.0 How can scientific methods help projects? Success Science improves results "The scientific method is an empirical method of acquiring knowledge that has characterized the development of science since at least the 17th century (with notable practitioners in previous centuries). It involves careful observation, applying rigorous skepticism about what is observed, given that cognitive assumptions can distort how one interprets the observation. It involves formulating hypotheses, via induction, based on such observations; experimental and measurement-based testing of deductions drawn from the hypotheses; and refinement (or elimination) of the hypotheses based on the experimental findings. These are principles of the scientific method." [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method]. We are not going to try to practice rigorous Nobel Prize Winning Science and discovery. illustrations.ocrText: Chapter 3. Levels of Sustainability Perception and Responsibility.15 The Ends-Means Levels We are presented with an apparently simple planning idea. There are 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals16, for us all, for the planet. The immediate decomposition, of every one of the 17 Goals, into 'Targets' tell us that there is a second level of detail there. And we are all well aware that the planetary reality is immensely complex. There are many indicators of that in the UN Plans. I have noticed that there is a persistent international and pervasive planning problem, whereby planners mix up, and confuse their ends (the future they really want), and a possible means (a specific strategy for reaching their ends). This ends-means confusion is bad for planning, because: (when you without further analysis, implement a particular means, because it seems to be your 'ends') 1. You risk implementing a means that does not achieve your ends. 2. You risk implementing a means that has bad side-effects on your other ends. 3. You risk implementing a means which takes far too much time, money or maintenance costs 4. Parties with hidden agendas can sneak in their agenda (a means) under cover of it being

illustrations.ocrText: Figure 3.3. Here is a diagram with the Poverty Goal decomposed, using the Goal 1 Targets as a suggested hint, at possible value dimensions, of 'Poverty'. These so-called 'Targets' (UN Speak) not only contain strategies, but also a hint as to 'Poverty' goal sub-value-dimensions worth managing. I am going to try to extract and define these ends & means ideas in the chapters below. We need to define these sub-goals, and see if they make sense and get approved. But this 'target decomposition' gives us a starting point. The other 16 Sustainable Development Goals (G2 to G17) are included, in the diagram above, to give the bigger picture of the whole problem area. They also need to be defined quantitatively, and approved. The strategies we suggest for G1 End Poverty cannot destroy or seriously disturb any of the other 16 Goals. Nor can Strategies for G1 End Poverty unjustly steal, limited common resources, for itself at the expense of the other 16 Goals. So we need somehow to keep track of all this. illustrations.ocrText: In general, I was never impressed [5, 27] with the expositions concerning Agile because of what I considered their "fuzziness". illustrations.ocrText: WHAT'S SO BAD ABOUT PLASTIC? The supplier recommends this design Sometimes suppliers have really valid reasons for recommending certain products or services. In which case we should be able to ask questions and get good answers: 1. Exactly why are you recommending this design to us? 2. Are there better alternatives, if we pay more, from you or others? 3. Can you give us some references from people who have used your recommendation 4. Are there any weaknesses with your recommendation that you do not think we care about? 5. What would you recommend if we said, we do not care about the initial cost as long as we get lifetime good quality from it? 6. Are you willing to give a total refund guarantee if we are unhappy with the design? 7. How many years have you been using that design? 8. Have you recommended this because we asked for a low bidder fixed price? You and I know that a supplier, might have unspoken reasons for recommending a design. illustrations.ocrText: That multi-dimensional design-evaluation process, will give us a more-complete view of the design situation, so that we can: • select the best mutually-exclusive architectures and designs. • Prioritize delivery of design components, so we can build a value-stream early, continuously and with good cost-effectiveness. Here is an explanation of the 'starting point' (all unknowns) for the Table above. I inserted a ?? at the intersection between a Requirement and the Main Design for each Requirement. Then I inserted a simple '?' for all the other potential impacts, which that Main Design might cause, like it or not; '?' for all the other Requirements, the 'Side Effects'. This ?-filled table is our 'initial state of ignorance', until we begin to estimate the potential impacts of our ideas on each value objective. '??' means we do not understand anything about the main effect of our Design on the main value, which it was chosen for 'good impact' on. '?' means we do not yet pretend to know anything about the side-effects of that idea, on all our other values. These side-effects could, theoretically, be so bad as to ruin our life! Confucius said: "True wisdom is knowing what you don't know.

illustrations.ocrText: Getting some rough idea of what we think we know about ideas: filling out the estimates without pushing your grey cells too much. Your Designs can have positive impacts (+), negative impacts (-) or no impacts (0). Your Designs can have minor impacts (+), medium impacts (++) or strong impacts (+++). So, we could subjectively, estimate what we think is the impact (pure opinion), based on our best available, in our head, knowledge and experience. Shaky stuff, but a beginning. We can potentially do this evaluation much better, more seriously, logically and quantitatively. But that might not be necessary, at this point, for something as 'insignificant' as your life, or .....? Some people prefer simple methods of evaluation. Which is fine if your problem is relatively simple, and the price of failure is not too high. So here is simple. But it is not good enough for less simple purposes. illustrations.ocrText: 7. Risk Management for Value Design 26. Risk in this book, means risk of things 'going wrong'. Estimating design impacts on a value table, reduces the risk of putting too much effort too early into low value, high cost, dubious design ideas 3. illustrations.ocrText: Chapter 1. What are 'Value Requirements'? (VR) Value Requirements are the most important requirements for any project. They are the main purpose, and main justification, for a project. They are the stakeholder's values. Value requirements start life as value 'attributes' needed by 'stakeholders'. No project can deliver all 'needed' values, by a deadline. No project will find all stakeholder values to be worth delivering. So all value requirements start life by being acknowledged as possible delivery candidates. But VRs need to go through an evaluation process to determine that we can prioritize them for real delivery. FUNCTION VALUE Figure 1.1 : A Value is a variable level of performance for a function. Represented graphically as an arrow emanating from a Function symbol. This is a simplified model, with a single value arrow. Reality is always that multiple values are needed concurrently. illustrations.ocrText: 1.1 Overview and Introduction Multi-dimensional thinking A 'Systems Engineering' tool Value Impact Estimation (VIE) is a free, open source, method, developed by this author during six decades of professional practice (1960-2022). The general purpose of VIE is to help evaluate any type of 'solutions' (like strategies, designs, architecture, sub-objectives) in relation to a set of stakeholder values and resource constraints. Put more simply, VIE is a tool to help us understand potential solutions to future values/costs objectives. VIE is a system engineering tool. That means it can be applied to any system. That means it uses logic, numerics, measurement, facts, experience, feedback, multiple values, and multiple cost aspects. illustrations.ocrText: 1.5 Summing up the VIE Introduction Logical fact-based decisions Value Impact Estimation (VIE) is a method for organizing clear factual detail, about values, costs, and strategies, into a web of insightful relationships. We will make estimates, based on evidence, and documented sources, regarding the perceived future impact, of any strategy (solution, design, idea, architecture), not only of the main value it is designed to impact, for example Security. But we can evaluate the side-effects, good and bad, on all other critical values, and all costs (of all types of long and short term resources). Like Usability, Maintainability. The estimates can be initial superficial approximations. But the estimates can be improved by more research, or getting feedback experience from earlier incremental implementations of smaller fractions (one city of many) of the strategy. illustrations.ocrText: 2.1 Stakeholder Value Specification basics Quantify future value levels Exactly how effective are your strategies in reaching your future performance levels? It is logically impossible to estimate the effectiveness of a strategy in relation to a vague performance requirement, like Extremely high Usability. To enable Value Impact Estimation to have any credibility in a logical engineering world, we have one unconditional need. We have to quantify the future value levels we want. Look at all the Customer Requirement examples in Figure 2.1. You can see that they are simply highly-vague words (Good Image, Keeps Presentation Flowing), with no agreed or specific meaning. This is a typical example of a wide-spread bad practice, Quality Function Deployment (QFD). Your common sense should tell you that is meaningless evaluation. illustrations.ocrText: 2.2 All Stakeholder Performance values quantified Engineering is numbers, not poetry Rule 1: define a numeric scale of measure for values. No exceptions Scale of Measure: a specified 'Scale' which defines a Value or resource, so that it can be used to define numeric points (Past, Goal etc.) on it. A Scale is defined once and reused by any levels of interest. illustrations.ocrText: 3.2 'Means' Decomposition How to decompose 1. Give value, 2. Independence. There are some very critical rules for strategy decomposition. Most people initially decompose into some work processes. They do not automatically know about these smarter, common sense, agile, rules. Rule 1. Decompose so that each sub-strategy will deliver planned measurable value increments, at each increment of it. Rule 2: Decompose, so that the sub-strategies can be implemented, in any valuable sequence. No dependencies in the the sub-strategies, at least - not for one decomposition tree. People pick this up quickly, and can always do it, same day. But they need to be instructed, and coached, and need to check their work. Check 1. Check 2: Can any one of the sub-strategies be delivered, before any of the others in the same sub-strategy tree set.? The reasons for these decomposition rules are: Reason 1. illustrations.ocrText: 3.5 'Means' Discovery Finding ideas Start from where you are, and evolve towards incredible value. It can be tempting, and marketeers and employees will try to tempt you: to design a major new system from the ground up. Experience shows that this 'big bang' approach will invariably fail completely or partly. It will cost far too much, not deliver the promised values, be delivered, if at all, years too late. Don't do it. Experience shows [21, MM] that the most competitive, successful, high-value and low-cost results are delivered, when you approach the problem incrementally. That means you start with existing systems, products, services, organizations. You change them one small step ('Quick Wins' Tom Peters calls them) at a time, and measure the effect. If the effect is not good enough, try a better strategy. If it works, accelerate. Elon Musk [21,MM] cites speed of iteration as a major competitive factor daily cycles). This means that the initial total architecture is staring you in the face. It exists, and you know a lot about it. It is stable. Hopefully, it is not already in total failure mode. illustrations.ocrText: 3.7 Design spec adjustment Fix bad specs The process of getting really well-written specs. Rare and difficult. Even a single word, like the word 'not' can radically change the effectiveness or efficiency of a strategy/design specification. Specifications need to be detailed enough to result in the best effectiveness and lowest costs. Specs need to be carefully written, and carefully reviewed and quality controlled [P42, Intel]. Intel requires maximum 0.2 defects per 600 words specified. That is almost superhuman. 'Human spec-capability' is 100x worse, at least. And even then, specs will be not as good as we hope for. The next step, after rigorous specification, is the subject of this book. Value Impact Estimation (VIE). This process will force us to think deeply about our specification, and whether it can confidently justify the effectiveness and costs, that we estimate. This VIE process will inevitably result in editing and correction of the design specifications. But, up to this point, it is guesswork; and nobody really knows very much about design attributes. illustrations.ocrText: 3.9 Getting Rid of Designs, as false 'ends' How to diplomatically get rid of your boss's favorite idea. Do you know the difference between 'ends' and 'means'? Hopefully. But it is not simple, because one level of organization's 'means' is often delegated to staff or suppliers, and becomes, from their point of view, their 'ends' (requirements, objectives). There is an old, 1576, saying: one man's meat is another man's poison. It is very common for an organization to adopt, as a so-called 'objective', some concrete artefact (digitalization, policies) rather than the real effect they want to achieve with that artefact. This is dangerous, because you might get the artefact, but not the result you wanted. The simple device to expose this situation is the question 'Why?' (Do you want that 'objective'). If there is an answer, like 'in order to get better (something)', then 'better something' is one step closer to what they really want. You can test this, by then saying. illustrations.ocrText: 4.1 Soft impact formats Simple Impact analysis We can be tempted to use a simplified impact table which as I have suggested, is appropriate in a personal 'life design' situation [3, LD]. And I commented on in 2.1 above, on Quality Function Deployment tables. These simplifications have a large number of weaknesses. These weaknesses can be forgiven if you are just trying to organise your thought process for a job offer, or an educational opportunity. Important for you. But not for anything as consequential as a 'national Health system', or a 'Military Weapon development'. We need to be aware of the total long-term consequences of our decision process, and then choose a method 'simple enough' to succeed [20, SU]. Let me remind you of the weaknesses of these simple impact tables, compared to the VIE we write about here. 1. The Value Objectives have no clear definition, magnitude or delivery constraint. 2. The Ideas (means, strategies) have no clear or detailed definition (so we don't know about costs and effects by 10X). 3. The impact estimates (0, ++, 2, -) are crude and intuitive. illustrations.ocrText: 4.3 Relative % impacts A neutral % metric - for a 'big picture' We let our PC convert from the Scale-Units to another metric: the '% increment' towards the target level. At first this might seem like just another way to say the same thing. It is, but this 'other way' has a very useful property, which the Scale-Units do not. We can fairly meaningfully add them up for different values and costs. This gives us a better overall picture, of all the impacts, that a single strategy has. And in addition, as we shall see later, we can add up the % impacts of a set of different but complimentary strategies, and decide if we have enough design ideas; or better, if we have enough with a safety margin. More about this below. These capabilities make it worthwhile, to introduce the % impact, and the computations required are without human effort. And 20 minutes saving, is equivalent to 50% of the way between Past and Goal (65 – 25 = 40, 20/40 = 50%). illustrations.ocrText: 4.16 Using VIE to drive deep team discussions If we have superficial discussion about our critical objectives and main strategies, we will almost certainly make bad decisions, and our projects will fail more. The moment we allow discussion to be based on pictorial slides, and their bullet-point poetic words (High Security, Block Chain AI) we will fail seriously to discuss meaningful ideas. We will draw wrong conclusions, and our projects are on a guaranteed failure path. The Value Impact Estimation method makes extensive use of the engineering rigour of Planguage in Competitive Engineering [2]. If you have large and complex projects, and you want to avoid failure, and to succeed [20, SU] you cannot allow yourself to use a childishly vague language, so typical of politicians and managers. You have to adopt thinking tools, from a culture which knows how to succeed in complex projects: engineering (meaning facts, feedback, metrics, logic). If you do not want to, or are incapable of it, then move aside. Collecting evidence to judge the credibility of an estimated fact¹. illustrations.ocrText: 4.20 Value Impact Estimation Principles Principles: Impact Estimation [2, CE] 2005. 1. The Principle of 'Words being difficult to weigh' Non-numeric estimates of impact are difficult to analyze and improve upon. A design idea described as 'excellent' could actually be worse than another merely described as 'good.' 2. The Principle of 'Doubtful digits are better than none' A bad numeric estimate, and its definition, can still be systematically criticized and improved. In fact, a random number is a better starting estimate than flowery, descriptive words. 3. The 'Evident' Principle Estimates without sources, evidence, and credibility are not evident. 4. The Principle of 'Uncertainty in no uncertain terms' The uncertainty estimate is at least as important as the main estimate. 5. The Principle of the 'Seat Belt' A safety margin is as necessary with uncertain estimates, as a seat belt is with uncertain traffic. 6. The Principle of 'Profitable Proposals' The value of an idea is 'how well it meets objectives'. The net value considers the costs too. 7.
